Uniform Title: *Kaulopaniṣad* Main Title: *Kaula Upaniṣads* with Commentaries by Bhāskarāya Secondary Titles: *Bhāvanopaniṣat*, *Śrīlalitāmahātripurasundaryupaniṣat* and its commentary titled *Bahvṛcavedīyā*, *Devīatharvaśīrṣopaniṣat*, and *Śrīkaulopaniṣat*
Notes: Data entered by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Mark S.G. Dyczkowski. Revision 0: Publisher: Aṣṭhāna Vidvan K.P. Nārāyaṇa Śāstrī;
Year of Publication: 1946.
Place of publication: Bangalore;
Country of publication: India.
Śrīḥ.
The Secret Essence of Meditation 1. The venerable Guru is the power that is the cause of all.
2. By that, the body consists of nine apertures.
Now, Bhāskararāya composes the ritual procedure for those very meditations that have been taught for the sake of liberation by means of the *Bhāvanopaniṣad*.

Having restrained the breath with the root mantra (mūla) and performed the three nyāsas beginning with the seer (ṛṣi), one should touch the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) while reciting: "Salutation to the venerable Guru, whose nature is the power of consciousness (cit-śakti) delimited by the faculty of discernment (viveka-vṛtti), and who is the essence of the Suṣumṇā."
Salutation to Prakāśānandanātha, whose self is the Sarasvatī of the right ear;
salutation to Vimarśānandanātha, whose self is the Śaṅkhinī of the left ear;
salutation to Anantānandanātha, whose self is Sarasvatī of the tongue.
Salutation to Śrī Jñānānandanātha, whose essence is Pūṣan in the form of the right eye;
salutation to Śrī Satyānandanātha, whose essence is Gāndhārī in the form of the left eye;
salutation to Śrī Pūrṇānandanātha, whose essence is Kuhū in the form of the banner.
Salutation to Svabhāvānandanātha, whose essence is the piṅgalā-nāḍī in the form of the right nostril; salutation to Pratibhānandanātha, whose essence is the iḍā-nāḍī in the form of the left nostril;
salutation to Sahajānandanātha, whose essence is the alambuṣā-nāḍī in the form of the anus.
Thus, having touched those respective locations,
[one contemplates] the Śrīcakra in the form of the nine wheels.
4. Vārāhī, in the form of a father, is the mother of the offering deity Kurukullā.
5. The human goals are the oceans. 6. The body is the island of the nine jewels.
7. It is endowed with the seven constituents, beginning with the skin, as well as the hair.
His intentions are wish-fulfilling trees; his splendor is a garden of eternal bliss.

Salutation to the body, which is the essence of the Śrīcakra consisting of nine wheels; salutation to Vārāhī, who is the essence of the bodily parts such as the bones, whose nature is that of the father;
salutation to Kurukullā, the deity of the *bali* offering, who is the essence of the bodily parts such as the flesh, whose nature is that of the mother.
*Namaḥ*. Having thus performed the pervasion three times,
[one offers] *namaḥ* to the Sugarcane Ocean, whose nature is the dharma situated in the rear part of the body.
Salutation to the Ocean of Wine, whose nature is the form of the right side of the body;
salutation to the Ocean of Clarified Butter, whose nature is the form of the eastern side of the body;
salutation to the Ocean of Milk, whose nature is the form of the northern side of the body, which is liberation.
Having performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*) three times with "Salutation to the island of the nine jewels for the self of the body," [one should perform it] as follows: 1.

Salutation to the island of the ruby (*puṣparāga*) for the self of flesh; 2. Salutation to the island of the sapphire (*nīla*) for the self of hair; 3. Salutation to the island of the lapis lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*) for the self of skin.

Homage to the one whose essence is blood, the island of coral gems; homage to the one whose essence is semen, the island of pearl gems; homage to the one whose essence is marrow, the island of emerald gems.
Homage to the Island of Vajra-jewels, whose essence is bone; homage to the Island of Gomedaka-jewels, whose essence is fat; homage to the Island of Padmarāga-jewels, whose essence is vitality.
1. Homage to the presiding deity of flesh, the Sovereign of the Kālacakra.

2. Homage to the presiding deity of body hair, the Sovereign of the Rudracakra. 3. Homage to the presiding deity of skin, the Sovereign of the Mātṛcakra. 4. Homage to the presiding deity of blood, the Sovereign of the Ratnacakra.
Homage!
9. The six seasons—sweet, sour, bitter, pungent, astringent, and salty—are to be contemplated by means of the tongue.

10. Knowledge is the offering of honor (arghya), the object of knowledge is the oblation (havis), and the knower is the priest (hotṛ); the worship of the Śrīcakra is the contemplation of the non-difference between the knower, knowledge, and the object of knowledge.

5. Salutation to the presiding deity of semen, the Sovereign Lady of the Ten Wheels (Daśācakreśvarī). 6. Salutation to the presiding deity of marrow, the Sovereign Lady of the Guru Wheel (Gurucakreśvarī). 7. Salutation to the presiding deity of bone, the Sovereign Lady of the Tattva Wheel (Tattvacakreśvarī). 8.
Salutation to the presiding deity of fat, the Sovereign of the Graha-cakra.
Salutation to the presiding deity of vital energy (ojas), the Sovereign of the Mūrti-cakra.
Salutation to the wish-fulfilling trees whose essence is volition. Salutation to the self of splendor.
Homage to Kalpakodyāna.
Homage to the spring season, whose essence is the sweet taste; homage to the summer season, whose essence is the sour taste.
Salutation to the rainy season, whose essence is the bitter taste; salutation to the autumn season, whose essence is the pungent taste;
salutation to the winter season, whose essence is the astringent taste; salutation to the cool season, whose essence is the salty taste.
Homage to the horses that are the senses and the self; homage to the elephants that are the sense-objects and the self.

Salutation to this moat of water, whose nature is compassion. Salutation to the ruby pavilion, whose essence is a mass of vital energy (*ojas*). Salutation to the special water offering (*viśeṣārghya*), whose essence is knowledge (*jñāna*).
Salutation to the oblation (*havis*), whose essence is the object of knowledge (*jñeya*). Salutation to the priest (*hotṛ*), whose essence is the knower (*jñātṛ*).
Salutation to the Consciousness-Self, the illustrious Mahātripurasundarī.
Thus, having bowed with the mind preceded by the contemplation of each respective [deity],

and having rested for a moment through the contemplation that dissolves the names and forms of the knower, the knowledge, and the object of knowledge, by realizing their nature as pure consciousness alone. (Fifteen)
One should worship the Nityās while placing the hand upon the heart:
1. Tripurā, 2. Tripureśī, 3. Tripurasundarī, 4. Tripuravāsinī, 5. Tripurāśrī, 6. Tripuramālinī, 7. Tripurāsiddhā, 8. Tripurāmbā, 9. [Tripurāmbikā].
In another tradition, Mahātripurasundarī is considered to be the nine sovereign goddesses of the cakras.
Salutation to the Nityā Kāmeśvarī, who is the lunar day (pratipad) and whose nature consists of one thousand four hundred and forty breaths.
Salutation to the Nityā Bhagamālinī, who consists of one thousand four hundred and forty-two breaths and is the form of the second lunar day (tithi).
Salutation to the Nityaklinnā-nityā, who is the form of the third lunar day (tithi) and whose nature consists of one thousand four hundred and forty breaths.
Salutation to the Nityā Bheruṇḍā, who is the form of the fourth lunar day, consisting of one thousand four hundred and forty breaths beyond that.
Salutation to the Nityā Vahnivāsinī, who is the fifth lunar day and whose nature consists of one thousand four hundred and forty breaths.
Salutation to the Nityā Mahāvajreśvarī, who is the form of the sixth lunar day (ṣaṣṭhītithi) and whose nature consists of one thousand four hundred and forty breaths (śvāsa).
Salutation to Śivadūtī Nityā, who is the seventh lunar day, consisting of one thousand four hundred and forty breaths.
Salutation to Tvaritā Nityā, who is the eighth lunar day, consisting of one thousand four hundred and forty breaths following that.
Salutation to Kulasundarī Nityā, who is the ninth lunar day (tithi) consisting of one thousand four hundred and forty breaths.
Salutation to Nityānityā, who is the tenth lunar day, whose nature consists of one thousand four hundred and forty breaths.
Salutation to Nīlapatākānityā, who is of the nature of one hundred and fourteen breaths plus forty more (1440), and who takes the form of the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī).
11. Niyati (destiny), the aesthetic sentiments such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), the supernatural powers such as *aṇimā*,
and those consisting of desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, envy, merit, and demerit— the eight [powers] beginning with the *brāhmī*.
The powers:
12. The ninefold support consists of the powers of the mudrās.
Salutation to Vijayā-nityā, who is the twelfth lunar day (tithi) and whose nature consists of one thousand four hundred and forty breaths following that;
salutation to her whose nature consists of one thousand four hundred and forty breaths following that.

Salutation to the eternal Jvālāmālinī Nityā, who is the thirteenth lunar day (trayodaśī), the embodiment of all auspiciousness; salutation to her who follows, whose essence consists of one thousand four hundred and forty breaths, and who is the fourteenth lunar day.
Salutation to the Nityā Citrā, who is of the nature of one thousand four hundred and forty breaths following that [period], and whose form is the lunar day (tithi) of the full moon.
Some also recite the mantras of the respective Nityās at the beginning of each; this is the meditation on the Nityās.

Or rather, it should be performed at the very end. Having performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) in the locations to be mentioned later with the mantra "Obeisance to the line of the first square" (*caturaśrādyarekhāyai namaḥ*).
Salutation to the essence of the peaceful rasa (*śānta-rasa*) in the form of the right buttock, for the attainment of the power of atomization (*aṇimā-siddhi*).
Salutation to the essence of the marvelous rasa (*adbhuta-rasa*) in the form of the tips of the fingers of the right hand, for the attainment of the power of levitation (*laghimā-siddhi*).

Salutation to the one whose form is the right hip, whose essence is the sentiment of compassion (karuṇa-rasa), for the attainment of greatness (mahimā-siddhi). Salutation to the one whose form is the tips of the toes of the right foot, whose essence is the heroic sentiment (vīra-rasa), for the attainment of lordship (īśitva-siddhi). Salutation to the one whose form is the tips of the toes of the left foot, whose essence is the sentiment of humor (hāsya-rasa), for the attainment of power over others (vaśitva-siddhi).
Salutation to the one whose form is the left hip and whose nature is the loathsome sentiment (*bībhatsa-rasa*), for the attainment of the power of irresistible will (*prākāmya-siddhi*).

Salutation to the one whose form is the tips of the fingers of the left hand and whose nature is the furious sentiment (*raudra-rasa*), for the attainment of the power of enjoyment (*bhukti-siddhi*). Salutation to the one whose form is the back of the left shoulder and whose nature is the terrifying sentiment (*bhayānaka-rasa*), for the attainment of the power of desire (*icchā-siddhi*).

"Obeisance to the form of the crest-base, whose essence is the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa), for the attainment of the *prāpti* siddhi; obeisance to the form of the back of the crest, whose essence is necessity (niyati), for the attainment of all desires;
obeisance to the line in the middle of the square"—having thus performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) within that.
Salutation to Brāhmī, whose nature is desire and who has the form of the two big toes;
salutation to Māheśvarī, whose nature is anger and who has the form of the right side; salutation to Kaumārī, whose nature is greed and who has the form of the head.
Salutation to Vaiṣṇavī, whose form is the left side and whose nature is delusion; salutation to Vārāhī, whose form is the left knee and whose nature is pride;
salutation to Indrāṇī, whose form is the right knee and whose nature is envy.

Having performed the pervasive placement within that [space], reciting: "Salutation to Cāmuṇḍā, the embodiment of merit in the form of the right outer spoke; salutation to Mahālakṣmī, the embodiment of sin in the form of the left outer spoke;
salutation to the final square line."
Salutation to the Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī Mudrā, whose nature is the thousand-petaled lotus below in the form of the two big toes;
salutation to the Sarvavidrāviṇī Mudrā, whose nature is the Mūlādhāra in the form of the right side.
Salutation to Śakti,
whose nature is the abode of the form of the head; salutation to the power of the Sarvākarṣiṇī mudrā.
Salutation to the power of the Mudrā who brings all under control, whose form is the left side and whose essence is the Maṇipūra [cakra].
Salutation to the power of the Mudrā who intoxicates all, whose form is the left knee and whose essence is the Anāhata [cakra].
Salutation to the power of the Sarvamahāṅkuśa mudrā, whose nature is the pure right knee;
salutation to the power of the Sarvakhecarī mudrā, whose nature is the supreme generative source of the right thigh.
Salutation to the Self in the form of Vāmoru-Rūpā, the power of all seed-syllables and mudrās;
salutation to the Self in the form of the thousand-petaled lotus above the dvādaśānta, the yoni-mudrā of all.
Salutation to the self of the nine supports in the form of the big toes; salutation to Tripurā, the mistress of the Heart-form Trailokyamohana-cakra, who is the seal (mudrā) of all three sections.
Having touched each of those respective places and contemplated all these as non-different from one's own self, one should meditate upon the indivisibility of the Self,
[offering] salutations to one's own self in the form of the manifest Yoginī for the attainment of the power of atomization (aṇimā-siddhi).

13. Earth, water, fire, air, ether, the ear, the skin, the eye, the tongue, the nose, speech, the feet, the hands, the anus, and the generative organ— these, along with the mind and its modifications, are the sixteen powers beginning with Kāmākarṣiṇī.

Or, one should meditate preceded by the ritual application: "Salutation to Aparicchinnasvātmātman, the Mudrā who agitates all. Then, having performed the pervasive placement (nyāsa) with "Salutation to the sixteen-petaled lotus," [one places it] upon the back of the right ear as the essence of Earth.
Salutation to Kāmākarṣiṇī-nityā-kalā, whose nature is the right shoulder;
salutation to Budhyākarṣiṇī-nityā-kalā, whose nature is the fire of the right elbow; salutation to Ahaṃkārākarṣiṇī-nityā-kalā, whose nature is the self.
Salutation to the self of the wind residing in the back of the right hand, the eternal digit that attracts sound;
salutation!

Salutation to the eternal digit (nityākalā) Rūpākarṣiṇī, whose essence is the space of the right thigh and who attracts touch; salutation to the eternal digit Rūpākarṣiṇī, whose essence is the hearing of the right knee and who attracts form; salutation to the eternal digit Rasākarṣiṇī, whose essence is the skin of the right ankle and who attracts taste.
Salutation to the eternal digit (nityākalā) Gandhākarṣiṇī, whose essence is the right sole of the foot and whose nature is the sense of smell;
salutation to the eternal digit Cittākarṣiṇī, whose essence is the left sole of the foot and whose nature is the sense of taste.

Salutation to the eternal digit Smṛtyākarṣiṇī Nityā, whose form is the left ankle and whose essence is speech. Salutation to the eternal digit Dhairyākarṣiṇī Nityā, whose form is the left knee and whose essence is the sense of smell.

Salutation to the eternal digit Nāmākarṣiṇī, whose essence is the form of the left thigh and the hands; salutation to the eternal digit Bījākarṣiṇī, whose essence is the form of the back of the left hand and the feet.
Salutation to the eternal digit Ātmākarṣiṇī Nityākalā, whose nature is the anus in the form of the left elbow;
salutation to the eternal digit Amṛtākarṣiṇī Nityākalā, whose nature is the generative organ in the form of the left shoulder.
Salutation to the eternal digit (Nityākalā), who draws the body [toward herself], whose form is distorted by the mind at the back of the left ear;
salutation to Tripureśvarī, the sovereign of the wheel that fulfills all desires in the form of the heart.
14. The eight [types of passion], beginning with Anaṅgakusuma, consist of the cognitions termed speech, grasping, movement, excretion, sexual pleasure, rejection, acquisition, and equanimity.

Alambuṣā, Kuhū, Viśvodarā, Vāruṇī, Hastijihvā, Yaśovatī, Payasvinī, Gāndhārī, Pūṣā, Śaṅkhinī, Sarasvatī, Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and Suṣumnā— these fourteen channels (nāḍīs) correspond to the fourteen powers (śaktis), beginning with Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī.
Salutation to the self-nature of the secret Yoginī, for the attainment of the siddhi of levity.
"Salutation to the Mudrā who dissolves all, whose own self is of an unenclosed form;
salutation to the eight-petaled lotus"— having thus performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) within that,
[one places] "salutation to Anaṅgakusumā, whose nature is speech in the form of the right conch."
Salutation to Anaṅgamekhalā, whose nature is the appropriation of the form of the right clavicle;
salutation to Anaṅgamadanā, whose nature is the movement into the form of the right thigh;
salutation to Anaṅgamadanāturā, whose nature is the emission in the form of the right ankle.
Salutation to Anaṅgarekhā, whose nature is the bliss of the form of the left elbow;

salutation to Anaṅgavegā, whose nature is the intellect called the relinquishment of the form of the left thigh; salutation to Anaṅgāṅkuśā, whose nature is the intellect called the material cause of the form of the left collarbone.
Salutation!
Salutation to Anaṅgamālinī, whose nature is the intellect known as equanimity (upekṣā) and who has the form of the left peak.
Salutation to Tripurasundarī, the sovereign of the heart-centered wheel that agitates all.
"Salutation to the Self in the form of the most secret Yoginī for the attainment of greatness;
salutation to the Self in the form of the unlimited for the Mudrā that attracts all;
salutation to the fourteen-spoked wheel"—having thus performed the pervasive placement (*nyāsa*) within that.
Salutation to the power Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī, whose essence is the Ālaṃbuṣā channel located in the central part of the forehead.
16. [Salutation] to Prāṇa, Apāna, Vyāna, Udāna, Samāna, Nāga, Kūrma, Kṛkara, Devadatta, ...
To the ten Vāyus beginning with Dhanañjaya, the deities of the outer ten-spoked [lotus] who bestow all accomplishments;
to the Śakti named Sarvavidrāviṇī, whose nature is the cavity in the right portion of the forehead, obeisance.
To the Śakti named Sarvākarṣiṇī, whose nature is Viśvodara located in the right cheek, obeisance.
Salutation to the Self in the form of Varuṇī on the right shoulder, who is the power that gladdens all.
Salutation to the power Sarvasammohinī, whose nature is the tongue of the elephant [Hastijihvā] located on the right side;
salutation to the power Sarvastambhinī, whose nature is Yaśovatī located on the right thigh.
Salutation to the self whose form is the milk-river of Dakṣa’s shanks, the power that causes universal yawning.
Salutation to the Śakti named Sarvavaśaṅkarī, whose essence resides in the left calf and who is Gāndhārī.
Salutation to the one whose nature is the beautiful Pūṣan with lovely thighs, and to the Śakti who delights all.

Salutation to the self in the form of Śaṅkhinī on the left side, to the power (śakti) Sarvonmādinī; salutation to the self in the form of Sarasvatī on the left shoulder, to the power Sarvārthasādhinī.
Salutation to the Śakti who fulfills all prosperity, whose form is the left cheek of Ātman.
Salutation to the Śakti who consists of all mantras, whose nature is Piṅgalā located on the left side of the forehead.
Salutation to the Śakti, whose nature is the Suṣumṇā located at the back of the forehead, who brings about the destruction of all dualities.
Salutation to Tripuravāsinī, the Mistress of the Wheel who bestows all auspiciousness in the form of the heart;
salutation to my own self in the form of the Sampradāya Yoginī, for the attainment of mastery.
Salutation to the Mudrā who brings all under her control, whose own self is of an undivided form.

Having performed the pervasive placement with "Salutation to the outer ten-spoked wheel," [one places] "Salutation to the Goddess who bestows all accomplishments, whose nature is the vital breath in the form of the right eye."
Salutation to the Goddess who bestows all prosperity, whose form is the downward breath (apāna) at the root of the nose.

17. Due to the differentiation of the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) caused by contact with these various winds, the digestive fire (jaṭharāgni) becomes fivefold through its primary function as the vital breath (prāṇa): namely, the expeller (recaka), the cooker (pācaka), the dryer (śoṣaka), the burner (dāhaka), and the saturator (plāvaka).

18. Kṣāraka, udgāraka, kṣobhaka, jṛmbhaka, and mohaka—these are the five types [of vital airs] according to their primary functions as serpents; residing within the bodies of humans, they digest the fivefold food consisting of what is chewed (bhakṣya), eaten (bhojya), sucked (coṣya), licked (lehya), and drunk (peya).

19. These ten deities of the fire-petals, beginning with Sarvajñā and located within the inner decagon, are saluted as the goddess Sarvapriyaṅkarī, who is the nature of the vyāna breath and the form of the left eye.
Salutation to the Goddess who brings about all auspiciousness, whose nature is the fire in the southeast corner of the belly;

salutation to the Goddess who grants all desires, whose nature is the samāna breath in the southwest corner of the belly; salutation to the Goddess who liberates from all suffering, whose nature is the serpent in the left knee.
Salutation to the Goddess who pacifies all death, whose self is the horse-headed Kūrma.
Salutation to the Goddess Sarvavighnavināśinī, whose self is the form of the right knee and the left shoulder;
salutation to the Goddess Sarvāṅgasundarī, whose self is the form of the left hip and the southeast corner.
Salutation to the Goddess who bestows all auspicious fortune, whose essence is the form of the conqueror of wealth located in the corner of the belly.
Salutation to Tripurāśrī, the sovereign of the Heart-form All-Accomplishing Wheel.
Salutation to one's own self in the form of the Kulakaula Yoginīs, for the sake of attaining the power of mastery (vaśitva).
Salutation to the Mudrā of Universal Intoxication, whose own self is the undifferentiated Self.
Having performed the placement (nyāsa) that pervades its interior with the mantra "Antardaśāracakrāya namaḥ" (Salutation to the Inner Ten-Spoked Wheel).
Salutation to Sarvajñādevī, whose nature is the fire of exhalation from the right nostril.
Salutation to the Goddess of All Powers, whose nature is the fire that digests and whose form is the palate of Dakṣa.
20. Cold, heat, pleasure, pain, desire, goodness (sattva), passion (rajas), and darkness (tamas)—these are the eight powers (śaktis) that exercise control.
Salutation to the Goddess who bestows all sovereignty, whose nature is the fire that consumes the right breast;
salutation to the Goddess who consists of all-knowledge, whose nature is the fire that burns the right testicle.
Salutation to the Goddess who destroys all diseases, whose self is fire that dries up the forms of the skin-disease known as sīvinī.
Salutation to the Goddess whose nature is the support of all, whose essence consists of the left testicle, form, alkali, fire, and the self.

Salutation to the Goddess Sarvapāpaharā, whose nature is fire and who manifests as the form of the left breast; salutation to the Goddess Sarvānandamayī, whose nature is fire and who agitates the form of the left cheek.
Salutation to the Goddess whose nature is protection from all [evils], who is the self of Vāmana, Nāsā, Rūpa, Jṛmbhaka, and Agni.
Salutation to the Goddess who bestows all desired fruits, whose nature is fire that deludes forms at the tip of the nose.
Salutation to Tripuramālinī, the sovereign of the wheel that provides all protection in the form of the heart.
Salutation to one's own self in the form of the Yoginī of the Inner Essence, for the attainment of the power of irresistible will.
Having performed the pervasive placement within that [space] with "Salutation to the one whose own self is of an undivided form; salutation to the Mahāṅkuśā-mudrā of all;
salutation to the eight-cornered wheel," [he places: "Salutation to Vaśinī, the goddess of speech, who is the nature of coolness in the right side of the chin."
Salutation to Kāmeśvarī, the goddess of speech, whose nature is heat and who takes the form of the right side of the throat.
Salutation to Modinī, the goddess of speech, whose nature is the bliss of the form on the right side of the heart.

Salutation to the goddess Vimalā-vāg-devatā, whose nature is the form of the right side of the navel and whose essence is suffering; salutation to the goddess Aruṇā-vāg-devatā, whose nature is the form of the left side of the navel and whose essence is desire.
Salutation to the victorious goddess of speech, whose essence is the quality of sattva, appearing in the form of the left side of the heart.
Salutation to the goddess of speech, Sarveśvarī, whose nature is the quality of rajas in the form of the left side of the throat.
21. The five subtle elements, beginning with sound, are the flower-arrows.
22. The mind is the sugarcane bow; 33. passion is the noose; 24. hatred is the goad;
25. the Unmanifest, Mahat, and Ego are the deities Kāmeśvarī, Vajreśvarī, and Bhagamālinī, who reside within the inner triangle.
Salutation to Kaulinī, the goddess of speech, whose essence is the quality of tamas in the form of the left side of the chin.
Salutation to Tripurāsiddhā, the Sovereign of the Wheel that removes all diseases in the form of the heart.
Salutation to the self-natured Self, whose form is the fire of the secret yoga, for the attainment of enjoyment.
Salutation to the Self of all Sky-faring Mudrās, whose own nature is of an undivided form.
Salutation to the all-piercing arrows, which consist of the five subtle elements (tanmātras) and take the form of the lower portion of the heart-triangle.
Salutation to those two [deities] on the right side of that, whose forms are mind and self, and who possess the bows that delude all.
Salutation to the two nooses that bring all under control, which consist of passion for the form of the portion above that.
Salutation to those two who are of the nature of aversion toward the form of that left side, and who are the goads that cause all [beings] to tremble.

Having performed the pervasive placement (vyāpaka-nyāsa) with "Obeisance to the Triangle-Cakra," [one places] "Obeisance to the Goddess Kāmeśvarī, whose essence is the Great Principle (mahattattva) in the form of the front portion of the heart-triangle."
Salutation to the Goddess Vajreśī, whose nature is the ego-principle (ahaṃkāra) located in the south-eastern corner.
Salutation to the goddess Bhagamālinī, whose nature is the Unmanifest (avyakta) situated in the form of the left corner.
Salutation to Tripurāmbā, the Sovereign of the Wheel who bestows all spiritual accomplishments and whose form is the heart.
Salutation to the Self, who is the form of the most secret Yoginī, for the fulfillment of one's desires.
Salutation to the Self of the nature of the undivided form, who is the seal of all seeds.
Having performed the pervasive placement (vyāpaka-nyāsa) with the mantra "Obeisance to the Wheel of Bindu" (binducakrāya namaḥ),
[one realizes that] unconditioned consciousness itself is Kāmeśvara.
27. One's own self, ever full of bliss, is indeed the supreme deity Lalitā.

28. The redness of all this is its contemplation (vimarśa). 29. And accomplishment is attained through one-pointedness of mind. 30. The metaphorical designation of "action" applies to creative contemplation (bhāvanā).

Salutation to Lalitā Mahātripurasundarī, the Supreme Deity, who is of the nature of the one Brahman consisting of existence, consciousness, and bliss, and who dwells within the heart of Kāmeśvara, whose form is the pure, unconditioned consciousness at the center of the heart.

Having contemplated that the very consciousness free from limiting adjuncts— which is of the nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss— reflected in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), is the redness of Lalitā, through the realization "I am indeed that [existence]."

Having contemplated the qualification of the limited consciousness (saṃvit) characterized by existence, consciousness, and so forth, as well as the absolute consciousness (kevalasaṃvit), through the relation of identity (tādātmya)— which takes the form of being constrained within the yantra of Kāmeśvara— by means of the relation of non-difference (abheda).
Pure consciousness itself, characterized by whiteness in the form of the absence of limiting adjuncts (upādhi), is the white conduct (śuklacaraṇa).

He is "red-footed" because he is characterized by passion (*rāga*), which takes the form of death consisting of the primordial supreme *I-consciousness* (*parāhaṃtā*) that is distinguished from the consciousness of the individual subject (*cit*).

Having contemplated that the state of being an object (viṣayatā) as determined by the mental modification in the form of "I" (aham-ākāra-vṛtti) regarding the two feet is indeed a mutual relationship of qualifier and qualified (viśeṣya-viśeṣaṇa-bhāva), which constitutes the perfect harmony (sāmarasya) of those two.
Salutation to Mahātripurasundarī, the Sovereign of the Wheel consisting of all bliss in the form of the Heart;
salutation to the Self of one's own nature in the form of the Yoginī of the supreme and non-supreme secret, for the attainment of the Siddhi of Prāpti.
Salutation to the one whose own self is of an undivided form, the seal of all wombs.
Thus, having correctly performed the mental contemplations preceded by the touching of each respective location, one should offer the ritual services (upacāras).
Just so, I contemplate the seat as being established in its own majesty, through the cultivation of that which is playful and unconfined.

I contemplate the offering of water for the feet (pādya), which is the washing with the water of meditation upon the formless nature of Existence-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānanda) of the impurity consisting of name and form residing in the foot, which is the gross manifestation beginning with the three worlds.
I contemplate the washing with water of honor (arghya) for that [Self], which has come into my hand in the form of subtle conceptual proliferation.
I meditate upon even the water in its form as mental cultivation as being the physical form of sipping water for consumption.
I contemplate the bath consisting of contact with the water of meditative cultivation, performed without cutting off any of its parts— such as existence, consciousness, bliss, and so forth.

I conceive of the cloth by means of the effacement of that specific objecthood belonging to the mental state consisting of cultivation which was attached to those very atoms, through the cultivation of its being non-objective to that mental state.

I offer these ornaments, which consist of manifold attributes such as being objectless, stainless, sorrowless, and immortal, by means of meditating upon their non-difference from the possessor of those attributes.
I bestow the fragrance that consists of the remaining pure consciousness alone, by removing the insentience of the earthly elements constituting my own body.
Likewise, by means of this meditation upon the portions of space, I offer flowers.
Likewise, with the thought of their being such, I fumigate the portions belonging to Vāyu.
In that same manner, by means of this process, I cause the fiery portions to blaze forth.
Having thus visualized them as portions of nectar, I offer them.
Likewise, through the meditation upon the lunar mandala at the end of the sixteen [fingers],
I perform the ritual preparation of betel.
I offer praise by means of contemplating the withdrawal of all words, beginning with Parā and Paśyantī, into Brahman through the medium of Nāda.
I circumambulate by dissolving into Brahman the mental fluctuations that run toward sense objects, thereby removing their dullness regarding those objects.
I bow down to them with single-minded devotion toward Brahman, by turning away from their respective objects.
Having thus performed the ritual service, one should offer oblations.

31. The dissolution within the Self of conceptual constructs such as "I" and "you," "existence" and "non-existence," "that which is to be done" and "that which is not to be done," "that which is to be worshipped," and so forth, is the *homa* (sacrificial oblation).
32. The internal offering consists of the meditation on the non-differentiation of the objects of meditation.
33. Observing the transformation of time in the form of the fifteen lunar days (tithis).
34. Thus, by being intent on meditation for three muhūrtas, two muhūrtas, or even a single muhūrtas, one becomes liberated while living; such a person alone is called a Śiva-yogin.
35. According to the Kādimata system, the internal meditations on the wheels (cakras) have been explained.
36. "He who knows thus has studied the Atharvaśiras. Thus ends the Bhāvanopaniṣad.
[The mental impressions] that have arisen regarding prescribed and prohibited objects—such as "I," "you," "the guru," "the deity," and so forth—[are to be dissolved].

I offer all those [energies]— which abide as the Wheel-King (*cakrarāja*) and consist of a multitude of infinite powers (*ananta-śakti*), as well as whatever subtle impressions (*saṃskāra*) they may be— into my own self, without emerging from samādhi, through the contemplation that all of them are nothing but pure consciousness (*cinmātra*).

I satisfy them all through the contemplation that all objects of meditation— beginning from my own nature and the vital breaths and ending with the multitude of powers such as the feet of the Guru— are of the sole nature of pure consciousness and do not differ from one another.
The wheel of lunar days (tithi-cakra), the wheel of time (kāla-cakra), and the wheel of space (deśa-cakra) exist in their aforementioned forms;
they are all beloved, shining, and real. Yet, I contemplate that everything which is expressed through name and form is indeed Brahman alone.

Alternatively, one should perform right here the previously described constant meditation (*nityābhāvanā*), which has the result of dissolving the breath; by means of that, through the contemplation of the identity of mind and wind, for three *muhūrtas*, two, or even one.
One should pervade [the body] uninterruptedly for a muhūrta; for such a person, the realization of oneness with the deity is attained, and the desired objectives are accomplished without effort.

Then, having descended [from the seat], performed three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma), and completed the threefold ritual placement (nyāsa) of the seers (ṛṣi) and so forth, one should praise the Guru; thus all is auspicious.
Thus has the ritual procedure been described by Bhāskararāya for the delight of virtuous people who have practiced the meditations taught in the *Atharvaśiras*.
O Śyāmā, mother of music, you who bear the primary burden of ministering in the abode of Paraśiva,
you who are expert in the gateway [of liberation], and whose own heart is filled with compassion— [protect] my [prayer].
Salutations to you, the Lady of the Glorious Lion Throne, who [rescues] those fallen into the forest-fire of existence and consumed by it, from their state of wretchedness.
Speak, you who have girded yourself in solitude to protect [us] with showers of nectar!
Where there is enjoyment, there is no liberation; where there is liberation, there is no enjoyment.
But for the preeminent practitioners of Śrī Sundarī, both enjoyment and liberation are held right in the palm of their hand.
Cast me into the netherworld, or establish me in the sovereignty of all the worlds;
O Mother, I shall not release your pair of feet, I shall truly not release them.
For those men who remember Him who is named Śiva and the Goddess who is Sarvamaṅgalā, there is victory and auspiciousness in every respect.
O Durgā, O Śivā, O Abhayā, O Māyā, O Nārāyaṇī, O Sanātanī!
O Jayā, grant me auspiciousness; salutations to you, O Sarvamaṅgalā! Thus [ends] the Śrī.
The supplementary verses for the sequence of the Great Sacrifice (*mahāyāgakrama*), as set forth in the *Bhāvanopaniṣad* in the thirty-fifth chapter of the *Śrītantrarāja*.

Now, listen to the instruction on the mental impression (*vāsanā*) regarding the sixteen *Nityās* as being one's own self, by which the accomplishment of identity with them certainly becomes manifest. (1)
The Guru is the primordial Śakti; she is considered to consist of reflective awareness (vimarśa).
Her state of novelty manifests as the "aperture" (randhra) of his body. || 2 ||
The offering goddesses (balidevyas) are one's own māyās; the fifth is Janakātmikā, and Kurukullā shall be the mother. The oceans are the [four] aims of human life (puruṣārtha). || 3 ||
The body is an island of jewels; its freshness consists of the elements and the hairs of the body; its volitions are the wish-fulfilling trees, and its own supports are known as the seasons. || 4 ||
The self of Time, facing westward by means of the wheel of planets, asterisms, and zodiac signs, thereby becomes oriented toward the east; other matters concerning the *pīṭha* have been told by me.
The knower is one's own self, knowledge is the precious offering, and the object of knowledge resides externally;
the worship of the Śrīcakra is said to be the unification of these three.

In the Śrīcakra, the supernatural powers (siddhis) are proclaimed, along with the tastes (rasas), Niyati, the waves (ūrmis), merit and demerit (puṇya-pāpa), and the Mothers beginning with Brāhmī. || 7 ||

Furthermore, the elements, the senses, and the mind are to be known as the eternal *akalās* in their respective order; likewise, the organs of action, their objects, and the defects are indeed the eight *śaktis*.
The fourteen channels are said to be the powers beginning with Kṣobhiṇī;
the ten vital airs are proclaimed to be the powers beginning with Sarvasiddhi.
The thirteen fires are said to be the powers (śaktis) beginning with Sarvajñā;
indeed, cold, heat, pleasure, pain, and desire are declared to be their qualities in sequence.
The powers (śaktis) are Vaśinī and the others; the subtle elements (tanmātras) are the flower-arrows; the mind is said to be the sugarcane bow, and passion is the noose. || 11 ||
O lady of excellent complexion, hatred is said to be the goad;
and in reverse order, they take the forms of the Unmanifest, Ego, and Mahat. (12)
The goddesses beginning with Kāmeśvarī are [the powers], while Saṃvit is known as Kāmeśvara;
one's own self alone is declared to be the deity, Lalitā, whose body is the universe. 13.
The redness is its reflective awareness (vimarśa); "worship" (upāsti) is the creative contemplation (bhāvanā);
"perfection" (siddhi) is the state of one-pointed mind; and "mudrā" is the contemplation of its sovereign power (vaibhava). || 14 ||

Even though there is movement, there is metaphorical designation because of being absorbed in that; diligence consists in the destruction of the causes of conceptual constructions within one's own self. (15)
The yantras and mantras everywhere serve as the means for achieving stability in one's own self-nature;
the worship of the Goddess during the junctions (sandhyās) constitutes immersion in Her from beginning to middle to end. || 16 ||
But those other powers that move within the wheel on all sides are declared to be the causes of all conceptual constructions. || 17 ||
Nyāsa is the conceptualization of one's own self as the deity within the body; japa is correctly described as the contemplation of the form of identity with that [deity]. 18.

The dissolution of all conceptual constructions within one's own self is considered the state of the human being; the contemplation of their mutual interpenetration constitutes their satiation. || 19 ||
The firm cessation within the Self of the sufferings of delusion, ignorance, and so forth, is indeed consecration; for the Self is the great substratum of all knowledge.

The absence of limiting adjuncts (upādhi) is called "instruction" (upadeśa); freedom from the distinction of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) is said to be "desire to hear" (śuśrūṣā), and steadfastness is called [the state of] stability. || 21 ||
The observation of the transformation of time in the form of lunar days (tithis)—these fifteen are eternal—is what has been declared as the Vāsanās. Thus [ends] the glory.
The Compendium of the Sixty-Four Services to Śrī Lalitā.
Oṃ! O Goddess Lalitā, supreme deity dwelling in the abode of the center of the heart, O Mother, I offer these sixty-four services to You with devotion. 1.
O Abode of the lap of Kāmeśvara, please accept this water for the feet with respect;
having removed your ornaments, I offer you fragrant oil.
Then, having entered the bathhouse and sat comfortably upon the jeweled pedestal there, perform the rubbing of your body with unguents.
Then, O Lalitā, I bathe you with warm water out of devotion;
thereafter, I consecrate you with the waters from golden jars.
O Maheśvarī, I offer you a cloth for wiping that has been washed, as well as uncolored silk garments, and a reddish upper garment for the breasts.
Then, O Supreme Goddess, having entered the unguent pavilion and seated yourself upon a golden throne, smear [the image] with fragrant pastes.
I shall fumigate the mass of hair with incense made of black agalloch wood,
and I offer garlands of flowers such as jasmine and all other seasonal blossoms.
Having entered the pavilion of ornaments and stood upon a golden throne, O Ambikā,
you compassionately placed the ruby crown upon your head.
O ocean of compassion, may a fragment of the full autumnal moon shine there; and adorn the parting of her hair with vermilion.
O Auspicious One, having applied a sectarian mark (tilaka) upon my forehead and collyrium to my eyes, O Mother, I also offer this pair of locks of hair to You with devotion. (10)
O Mother, I offer you the jeweled earrings, as well as the nose-ornament;
O Goddess, I place a pair of earrings and lac upon your lips.
The primary ornaments include the *sauvarṇacintākapadaka*,
the *mahāpadaka*, the *muktāvalī*, the *ekavalī*, and other such jewelry.
"O Mother, accept this pair of armlets;
likewise, O graceful Ambikā, accept this series of bracelets and the finger-ornaments. (13)
O beautiful one, Oḍyāṇa is at the end of the waist;
there is also the girdle, the ornament of good fortune, the anklet for the feet, and the pair of bells. (14)
O Mother of the World, I offer a ring at your feet;
likewise, I offer a noose in your upper left hand and a goad in your right hand.
And likewise, O beautiful one, hold in your other left hand a bow made of sugarcanes,
and in your right lower hand, hold flower-arrows.
And I place the ruby sandals upon the feet of Śivā;
O Supreme Śiva, ascend with joy to the discus along with the protective goddesses.
O Tripurasundarī, together with those [attendants] who possess identical dress and ornaments,
she is seated there upon the lap of Kāmeśa in the paryaṅka posture.
I always worship you, who are delighted by the drinking of the nectar-liquor;
perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) once more with the pure water of the Gaṅgā.
Then, O Mother, place a camphor betel-roll in Your mouth,
Your lotus-face radiant with a smile of blissful exultation.
When will the fortunate man, remembering you—the wish-fulfilling creeper for the devoted—perform the auspicious *ārārtika* ceremony, [offering] a parasol, a fly-whisk, and likewise a mirror? (21)
I offer you a palm-leaf fan, as well as perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps.

Divine food, filled with ghee, soups, and vegetables, combined with various kinds of exquisite dishes, along with milk-rice mixed with honey, sugar, and curd, was placed in thousands of vessels made of refined gold from Śrī Kāmeśvara and set upon trays of rubies.
One should cause the food offering (naivedya) consisting of black gram cakes, flour cakes, and other such items to be presented. || 22 ||
May the Mother Lalitā, who resides in the center of the heart, be well-pleased by these sixty-four offerings described in the twenty-one verses beginning with "Sāgra."
In the year known as Śrīmukha, during the bright fortnight of the month of Tulā,
on the fourth lunar day in the afternoon, his mind was entirely dedicated to Lalitā.
With twenty-one verses, Nārāyaṇa joyfully accepted the sixty-four modes of service for the pleasure of Parāmbā.

The virtuous Nārāyaṇa, son of Śrī Puruṣottama, composed this [work on] the worship of the Goddess, which grants all desires, in the city of Mahīśūra; may she who rests upon the left lap of Kāmeśvara be pleased. 26.
Ātatsat. Śrī. Thus ends the compendium of the sixty-four modes of worship (ṣaṭcatvāriṃśad-upacāra) for the Goddess.
It is complete.

Now follows the recitation of the Peace Mantra (*śāntimantra*) of the Tripuropaniṣad, together with its commentary: Om! May my speech be established in my mind; may my mind be established in my speech.

My speech, engaged in the recitation of texts that expound the knowledge of reality, is always established in my mind; that is to say, the mind is the conveyor of the entire collection of words intended to be spoken.

And my mind is established in speech; that is to say, the collection of words that conveys the knowledge of the Self is intended by the mind for expression. For when speech and mind mutually support one another, they are able to comprehend the entire text concerning the meaning of knowledge in its completeness.

The sense is that if there is a lack of attentiveness of the mind, one might say something incoherent; likewise, if there is a lack of dexterity in speech, what is intended to be said is not articulated correctly. Therefore, a prayer for mutual conformity between these two is made.
Be manifest to me again and again.
By the word *āvis*, the self-luminous Brahman-consciousness is expressed. "O Supreme Self, *āviredhi* unto me"—the meaning is: "be manifest to me by removing the veil of ignorance."
Be the axle of my Veda; what I have heard, do not let it slip away from me.
O Speech and Mind, you two must be capable of bringing to me— that is, for my sake— the Vedic texts which expound the knowledge of reality (*tattva-vidyā*). O organ of hearing,
do not abandon the collection of texts heard by you for my sake.
The meaning is that one should forget it.
By means of this which has been studied, I join together days and nights; I shall speak the Ṛta;
I shall speak the Truth.

By means of this Upaniṣadic text, which has been studied and not forgotten, I join together the days and nights; that is to say, having abandoned sloth both by day and by night, I recite it continuously. And when the text has been recited, [it becomes] *ṛtam*—that which is the supreme reality.

I shall speak the truth (*vastu*); the meaning is that there may never be a speaking of a contrary matter. *Ṛtam* is mental, and *satyam* is verbal; the meaning is that having reflected upon the reality of the thing with the mind, I shall speak it with speech.
May that protect me; may it protect the speaker; may it protect me; may it protect the speaker; may it protect the speaker. Om. Peace, peace, peace.
May that reality of Brahman protect me, the disciple, through perfect awakening;
and may it protect the teacher by bestowing the capacity for awakening others.
Furthermore, the prayer for the fruit—"May you protect me once again"—is directed toward the cessation of ignorance;

however, for the teacher, the fruit is the attainment of the non-interruption of the tradition of knowledge (*vidyā-sampradāya*) through the acquisition of such a disciple. By means of this recitation of the mantra...
First, the obstacles that hinder the acquisition of knowledge are removed; however,
after the arising of knowledge,
the obstacles that produce non-belief and contrary conceptions [are removed].
The repetition indicates the conclusion of the chapter. Thus ends the meaning of the *śānti* mantra.
Prosperity!
In the *Śrī Tripuropaniṣad* (with commentary):
"While my own Lord’s two lotus feet exist within the thousand-petaled lotus of my heart,
how can there be such statements as 'the production of a lotus from a lotus has never been seen'?"
Those who perform their rituals according to the rules of the *Śrīsāṃkhyāyana-kalpasūtra*, whose collection of mantras is the *Śākala* [Saṃhitā] and whose Brāhmaṇa is the *Kauṣītaki*,
by those students of the Ṛgveda is recited that expansion of mantras found in the middle of the Āraṇyaka.
With sixteen Rigvedic verses, we shall expound that Great Upaniṣad.
Indeed, in this world, the Veda to be studied by those belonging to the three twice-born castes is twofold, distinguished as the Pūrva-kāṇḍa and the Uttara-kāṇḍa.
Both types of that [scripture], whether directly or indirectly, are engaged in the prescription of specific actions.

Furthermore, some ritual actions have deities, while others are deity-less—such as the *agnihotra* sacrifice, ritual bathing, and so forth; and likewise, the worship of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, the worship of the sacrificial fire by women, and so on.

Just as those who possess the conviction that there exists a self distinct from the body, capable of traveling to and returning from the next world, are qualified for actions whose fruits are realized in the hereafter,
so too are they [qualified] in these [present matters].
Only those who possess faith— that there exists some deity capable of bestowing desired fruits, even though invisible to people like us—
are qualified for the worship of Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and others. It is precisely with reference to such a disposition of people that [the following was said]:

The fivefold nature of the deities, beginning with their corporeal form, has been established by Bādarāyaṇa and others. However, those who lack confidence in the actual existence of deities— due to the influence of the karma of previous births— and yet possess a sense of faith (āstikatā), are qualified only for the ritual acts taught in the Pūrva-kāṇḍa, and not for this.

In the context of the worship of deities, it was precisely with the intention of such people that Jaimini and others established the doctrine of the primacy of ritual action (*karma-prādhānya-vāda*) by refuting the fivefold attributes of deities, such as their corporeal forms. For this very reason, [this applies] only to those ritualists of that kind.

In the *Mṛgendrasaṃhitā*, it is described in the commentary (*vṛtti*) that when a few individuals, due to the ripening of their karma, engage in the worship of Śiva and Śakti, they are subjected to ridicule for abandoning the Mīmāṃsaka doctrine. Furthermore, even those who are worshippers of deities [must acknowledge] the embodied form (*vigraha*) and so forth.
Even by those who understand the secret intent behind the negation of the five [sheaths],
the doctrine of the primacy of karma must not be rejected; for if it were so rejected,
such practitioners would lack the specific maturation of the mind required [for higher realization].
Because trust does not arise in an object that is being contested,
and because doubt arises regarding the object they rely upon due to the arguments for its refutation, they fall into the calamity of losing both positions. For this very reason, of those...

For the sake of preservation alone, even lay followers (upāsakas) must perform those same actions with full confidence, exactly as [the monks do]. It is with this very intention that injunctions such as "Even considering the welfare of the world, you ought to act" were taught. Not otherwise.
And there are prohibitions such as, "One should not cause a division of mind among the ignorant who are attached to action," and so forth; for even by those who have ascended to a higher stage,
the lower stage must be maintained with effort through their own stage.
The condensed meaning, however, is that non-disclosure must necessarily be practiced.

By this, it is established that these two—prescription and prohibition—are necessary even for those who are liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) and who walk upon the path beyond the three qualities (*niṣtraiguṇya*). As for those who, over many lifetimes...
In those individuals for whom a firm distinction in the ripening of the mind is observed due to the power of performing the practices previously mentioned in Koṇḍa,
one must examine them thoroughly and gradually reveal [the teachings] belonging to their own level; otherwise, [it would lead to harm].

Because it would result in the interruption of the tradition. Those various stages (*bhūmikā*) culminating in the worship of Tripurasundarī have been demonstrated by us in detail in our commentary on the *Vāmakeśvaratantra* titled the *Setubandha*. Regarding the scriptures of worship (*upāsanā-śāstra*), however—
The deity alone is primary; the ritual action is not primary.

Precisely because action lacks primacy, the Vedāntas are the means for realizing the established reality that is the form of the deity; such is the logical conclusion. And the deity has three forms—the gross, the subtle, and the supreme. Among these, the first is described in the verses on their respective meditations, while the second—
The third, however, consists of the respective root mantras and is of the nature of latent impressions (vāsanā).

Precisely because the forms of the deity are threefold, its worship is also threefold, distinguished as external sacrifice (*bahiryāga*), recitation (*japa*), and internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*). This very [teaching], along with its ancillaries, the *Ṛgvedapuruṣa* teaches in the form of the *Mahopaniṣad*, beginning with the words "three cities" (*tisraḥ puraḥ*).
By the phrase ending with "ityupaniṣad," the application (viniyoga) of this Upaniṣad is to the Supreme Deity (paradevatā),
according to the indicative mark (liṅga) of the mantra consisting of the third and tenth verses.
There are three cities with triple paths, frequented by all people, where the imperishable syllables are firmly established.
Having presided over this ageless and ancient one, the greatness of the deities is most exalted.
In that regard, in order to point out the principal deity, he recites the first verse beginning with "tisraḥ puraḥ" and so forth.

In that regard, liberation (mukti) is fivefold: first, *sālokya* (residing in the same world); then the triad of *sāmīpya* (proximity), *sārūpya* (similarity of form), and *sāyujya* (union); and finally, *kaivalya* (absolute isolation). Among these, the first and the last each have two paths, while the middle three have one path. And so it is said:
The Taittirīyas record: "He who, knowing this, dies during the northern course of the sun, having attained the greatness of the gods, goes to union with the Sun;
but he who dies during the southern course, having attained the greatness of the ancestors..."
He attains union with and residence in the same world as the Moon. A Brāhmaṇa who knows this indeed conquers these two glories of the Sun and the Moon;
therefore the Brāhmaṇa attains glory; therefore the Brāhmaṇa...
"Greatness"— this is the sense: for those of perpetual celibacy (*ūrdhvaretas*) who perform the duties prescribed for their own stage of life (*āśrama*),
the attainment of the world of the Moon (*candraloka*) takes the form of *sālokya* (residing in the same world) through the meditation on the symbol (*pratīkopāsanā*).

Through meditation on the relationship of owned and owner, and through meditation on the "I-grasp" (ahaṃgraha), there is the attainment of the world of Āditya in the form of the triad beginning with proximity (sāmīpya).

However, for one who possesses the knowledge of Brahman in the form of the worship of the attributeless (nirguṇa), there is the attainment of the state of Brahman in the form of absolute liberation (kaivalya). This very triad of paths is clearly elaborated in the third part of the Viṣṇupurāṇa. [The following is] the subsequent [verse]:
From the passage beginning with "That which is south of Agastya and the Ajavīthī is the path of the ancestors (pitṛyāṇa),

indeed that path is outside the path of Vaiśvānara," and ending with "and that is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu, perceived through the vision of discriminative knowledge," it is established that there are precisely three paths.

The three cities (pura) are also to be traversed; because she leads one to these three such cities, or because she is their very form, the Supreme Deity is called Tripurā. By worshipping her through the intellect of the Self as a symbol, through the intellect of the Mother, through the "I"-consciousness, or even through ritual action, a mortal attains absolute liberation (kaivalya).

"one attains the *padam*. Since it is stated by this passage from the *Śaktirahasya* that the attainment of Tripura occurs even through the worship of the fivefold self, therefore she alone is the three cities (*tisraḥ puraḥ*), Tripurā; and she is the "three-pathed" (*tripathā*), she whose paths are three.

In the case of *tatpuruṣa* compounds ending in *pathin*, neuter gender does not apply by virtue of the suffix *-ṇī* itself, according to the rule *pathaḥ saṃkhyāvyayādeḥ*. The word *carṣaṇi* is a Vedic synonym (*nighaṇṭu*) signifying "offspring" (*prajā*). Thus, it refers to that [goddess] in whom all (*viśvāḥ*) beings (*carṣaṇayaḥ*) reside.
"Viśvacarṣaṇī" means the goddess who is the progenitor of all living beings.

Alternatively, this is what must be understood here: that very first contemplation (*īkṣaṇa*) of Brahman, established by the Śruti in the passage, "It [Brahman] thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate,'" is itself the progenitor of all;
it is of the nature of desire (*icchā*) and also of the nature of action (*kṛti*). "It desired" (*sā aikṣata*).

From another Vedic scripture, "He performs austerity" (*tapo kurute*), it is understood that even by the statement "His power of knowledge and action is innate" (*svābhāvikī jñānabalakriyā ca*), it is established that there is only one primordial function (*vṛtti*) non-different from Brahman,
consisting of the forms of knowledge, will, and action. That [function]...
Vṛtti itself is called "quiescent" because it consists of the collective totality of will, knowledge, and action.
She is called *Parā* because she is the subtle form that is the aggregate of the triad of Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and Vaikharī;
she is called *Ambikā* because she is the aggregate form of Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī. She...
The deity whose nature is peace is indeed the Bindu-cakra situated within the Śrīcakra. This has been stated in the *Nityāhṛdaya*, beginning with the exposition of the Supreme Brahman:
The Wheel of the Bindu (baindava-cakra) and so forth is the abode of the waves of the universe, pervaded and consisting of the three Mothers.
And that very [reality] is designated by the three qualifiers as "the three cities," "the threefold path," and "pervading all people. Regarding these qualifiers,
through the use of both the plural and the singular, [the nature of] the qualified [subject] is indicated.
The state of having three forms and the state of being a single essence have been indicated.
Concerning Brahman as delimited by such a vision,
it is also stated in the Kālikā Purāṇa:
Her maṇḍala is a triangle, and her city-gate (bhūpura) consists of three lines;
her mantra is said to have three syllables, and likewise her form is threefold.
The Kuṇḍalinī energy is threefold for the creation of the three deities.

"Because there are three triads in every [aspect], she is therefore considered Tripurā. Having thus indicated her as the generator of the creation of meaning (*arthasṛṣṭi*), he indicates her also as the generator of the creation of sound (*śabdasṛṣṭi*) with the words "wherein" (*yatra*). "Wherein" means in her who consists of the forms of Śāntā, Ambikā, and so forth.

In Tripurā, the vowels beginning with *a*, the consonants beginning with *ka*, and those beginning with *tha*—sixteen syllables each—are situated there. These syllables are perfectly and thoroughly established, like a tree within the seed of a banyan. Indeed, it is the letter *ha*.

Because of the statement: "The phoneme *ha*, which is of the nature of *kalā* and called *vimarśa*, is proclaimed to be none other than the very essence of *vimarśa*; therefore, it is not grasped separately as an individual form (*vyaṣṭi*). However, the phoneme *la* is not distinct from the phoneme *ra*. As for the phoneme *kṣa*, it is indeed of the nature of a combination of *ka* and *ṣa*.
It is independent. Therefore, there are forty-eight *mātṛkās*. These indeed are the *mātṛkās*. And so it is stated in the *Sūta-saṃhitā*:
"Existing in one way, in two ways, and likewise in sixteen ways..."
I bow to that supreme *kalā* which is divided into thirty-two varieties. Thus.

It is twofold through the distinction between vowels (*svara*) and consonants (*vyañjana*); the meaning is that the vowel has sixteen forms and the consonant has thirty-two divisions. In the two-word phrase beginning with "akṣara," the substitution of *jas* for *śas* is a Vedic (*chāndasa*) anomaly. Thus, by means of the first half [of the verse].

Having taught the essential nature of the Bindu-cakra, he speaks of the Supreme Deity who presides over it and is to be worshipped, saying: "Adhiṣṭhāya" (presiding over). There is a certain Deity who, having presided over this Tripurā—who has just been taught as being of the form of the Bindu—[remains there].

According to the statement of Kātyāyana, "The verb *as* (to be), followed by *bhavanti*, exists even when not explicitly employed in the first person," there is an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) of the verb *as*. Alternatively, it may be construed with the action expressed in the subsequent mantra. That deity is ageless, being devoid of death.
In the context of the root *jṛ* meaning "decay of age," the term "decay of age" (*vayohāni*) refers specifically to the destruction of one's lifespan.
"Ancient" (*purāṇī*) means beginningless. Among the most renowned deities—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others—she is the greatest.

She is the most excellent; she is of the same nature as the majesty of those deities. The sense is that this very [Goddess] is the source even of the greatness of other deities, for it is through meditating upon her alone that they attain their majesty.
Since numerous instances are shown in the Tripuropaniṣad and in the Purāṇas, Tantras, and other texts following it, of Vidyās worshipped by Śiva, Viṣṇu, and others, [it is said]:
"Śambhu worships the auspicious Goddess, who consists of the power of mantra."

This is because the various types of images worthy of worship by all the gods are described in detail in the *Padma Purāṇa*. Furthermore, it is according to the maxim: "A beggar ought not to beg from another beggar, provided there is another who is not a beggar."
The implied meaning, however, is that the worship of the Supreme Deity alone is superior to the worship of other deities;
this very point was stated by us in the *Paraśivastava*.
Since you possess the sovereignty granted by you, how could you beg from other lords of the gods— those who are like mendicants, headed by Śakra,
Brahmā, and Hari— to say "give"? How could you seek such things from others when you are a partaker of the power bestowed by the Supreme Śiva?
I am a mendicant; though ignorant, I am also the *ukthya* sacrifice, which is a constituent part of a hundred variations of the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāhakra-tu*).
It desires the characteristics of the Jyotiṣṭoma and Ukthya sacrifices, but not the characteristics of the Dvādaśāha Ukthya.
By means of Vedic signs such as "the goat" (aja) and so forth, [it refers to] the deity presiding over the bindu and cakra.

It is stated that [the Supreme Self] is indeed the Supreme Brahman. The feminine gender [of the word *devatā*] is intended to indicate its status as the substantive (*viśeṣya*); for this very reason, there is a neuter designation in another Śruti. And thus, it is clearly stated by the Atharvaṇas:
They declare:
"The city of Ayodhyā of the gods has eight wheels and nine gates; within it is a golden treasure-chest."

The heavenly world is enveloped in light; within that golden, three-cornered sheath, it is established in a triple foundation. Whatever therein possesses self-consciousness, that indeed the knowers of Brahman know.

Above the eight wheels, beginning with the *bhūpura* and ending with the triangle, there is a sheath (*kośa*) which is to say, a *bindu* that contains within it three forms. Within that is a great being (*mahadbhūta*) called a *yakṣa*. It is designated by the term *yakṣa* because it is unfit for external worship.
Only those who know Brahman know that within their own self; no others do—this is the meaning. Such is the detailed explanation in the *Setubandha*.

Having thus described the *binducakra*, the second verse is spoken in order to teach the wheel consisting of nine wombs (*navayoni*), which is the composite form of the triangle, the eight-cornered [figure], and the two curves. It begins with the words: "The nine wombs... (*navayonīḥ*).
They have assumed nine wombs, nine wheels, nine indeed as yogas, and nine yoginīs.
She is the sovereign lady over the wheel of the nine, auspicious with the nine mudrās and the nine blessed ones,
the mistress of the earths.

They have established three cities with nine wombs; though it is a single *binducakra*, it assumes a triple form in each because it consists of a triad—this is a form derived from the Vedic root *dīdhīṅ* (meaning "to shine" and "to play"). And its illumination (*dīpana*) is as follows:
In this context, the intended meaning is that manifestation itself is, in effect, production.

Within the limitation of Śāntā, he brought forth the three deities— will-power (icchā-śakti), action-power (kriyā-śakti), and knowledge-power (jñāna-śakti); and within the limitation of Ambikā, he generated Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra in female form, named the powers Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī.

The meaning is that the goddesses of speech—namely Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and Vaikharī—generated [the letters] by means of their respective delimiters (*parātvāvacchedena*). Alternatively, the syntactical connection is: "That very Supreme Deity, presiding over this Tripurā, created the nine *yoni*s. These are indeed the nine deities themselves.

The path of latent impressions (*vāsanādhvan*) consists in their being transformed into the nature of the wheel of the nine wombs (*navayonicakra*). Furthermore, the nine wheels, such as the *Trailokyamohana* and others—whether already arisen or yet to arise—exist within the nine wombs themselves in the form of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). This is what he expresses by the words "the nine wheels."

"They have assumed nine wombs as their agents"—thus, by means of two power-triangles (śaktitrikoṇa) and one fire-triangle (vahnitrikoṇa), the nine-womb wheel (navayonicakra) is produced. Since there are three lines for each triangle, the conjunctions of these nine lines likewise result in nine forms of triangles. Therefore, they have assumed nine yoginīs.

The sense is that because the nine wheels exist here [in this body], the group of nine Yoginīs located therein—beginning with Prakaṭā—also exists right here within the nature of the corners. This is because of such conventional expressions as: "That supreme light above is unconditioned by space and time."

It is understood that the manifestation of the *bindu*-wheel (*binducakra*) and so forth, delimited by space and other factors, exists below and beneath Brahman. It is precisely based on this that the "expansion of Meru" (*meruprastāra*) of the Śrīcakra is established. Therefore, within a single cakra, everything from the outer enclosure (*bhūpura*) up to the *bindu* [is contained].

Above and above are the nine levels (*bhūmikā*s), and their presiding deities are also named Tripurā, Cakreśvarī, and so forth; they are not otherwise. He states that these too abide within the nine wombs (*yoni*) in a subtle form: "In the wheel of the nine..."

"Even the sovereigns of the earth have established nine wombs as their creators. The term "Syonā" (the Auspicious) is an epithet of Cakreśvarī; its meaning is "she who is the cause of happiness. The nine mudrās, beginning with Saṃkṣobhiṇī and ending with Yoni, are also situated right here. However, the "Nine Auspicious Ones" (Navabhadra) are [described] in the Tantra.
"Dharma and adharma, as well as the selves, the means of knowledge (mātṛ), the objects of knowledge (meya), and likewise light—thus [it is said].
The meaning of this is a group of nine: merit, demerit, the self, the inner self, the supreme self, the self of knowledge, the knower, the object of knowledge, and valid cognition.
The detailed exposition of the nature of the fourfold self is to be found in the Ātmopaniṣad.

"This wheel consists of nine aspects and possesses ninefold divided mantras," according to the observation in the *Upabṛṃhaṇa*. Alternatively, the mantras may be understood by means of the term "Bhadrā.
Regarding these, some say they are the mantras of the nine Mistress-of-the-Wheel (Cakreśvarī) deities; others say, due to their proximity, they are indeed the mudrā-mantras.

This is indeed appropriate. The condensed meaning is that within the very *saṃhāracakra*—which consists of the three wheels (*cakras*) in the form of the point (*bindu*), the triangle, and the eight-cornered figure—the entire *śrīcakra* exists in a subtle form. This applies to the methods of abbreviated worship during times of distress.
The ritual procedure for the worship of the deities, beginning with Vasu and Koṇa and ending with Bindu, which is found in the Tantras— of that,
this very [Vedic] scripture is the root authority. In all these cases,
the corroborative statements from the Tantras and Purāṇas are not written here for fear of prolixity.
Now, in order to teach the wheel of maintenance (*sthiticakra*), which consists of two tens and two *anvaśras*, he recites the third verse:
(3) "She was one; she was nine; she was nineteen; she was twenty-nine."
May the forty-three kindling-sticks enter [the fire] like longing mothers.
From these nine sources, it was said, "One breathed, sighing," the tenfold group of elements arose—namely, the five subtle elements and the five gross elements.
From those, through the distinction of gross and subtle, the tenfold group of objects such as sound and the limbs of the body arose; and from those...

The five organs of action, the five organs of knowledge, and the four internal organs—thus the fourteen were born. All these deities, being female in form, are indeed of the nature of the womb (*yoni*). All this [is as follows]:
"The group of ten consisting of the gross elements (*bhūta*) and the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), by virtue of being the objective support for manifestation,

has its form as the throbbing twelve-spoked [wheel] explained in the Tantra" and so forth. That very same procedure is taught here, preceded by a restatement of what was previously mentioned, beginning with "that which is the first."

In the beginning, she alone existed as the cause of the entire world, in the form of the *bindu*-wheel (*binducakra*). Then she became ninefold, by way of the nine *yoni*s. Then she became nineteenfold, consisting of the nineteen *svarūpa*s; namely, the nine *yoni*s and the ten internal *daśāra-yoni*s.

The word "twenty" (*viṃśat*) and so forth is Vedic [in form]. Then, by the union of the twenty-nine [petals] with the ten external *yoni*s, there are thirty-nine. Then, by the union of the forty-three—consisting of the three [inner petals] and the fourteen [outer ones]—with those in the east, there is a single form consisting of forty-three *yonis*.

The meaning is that the Goddess has been born. Because the Bindu-cakra is of the nature of the internal space (*antarākāra*), it is not enumerated among the "single-seated" (*ekāsana*) forms shaped like a womb (*yonyākṛti*). Kindled by fuel, blazing brightly—may these [energies] enter me this morning; may they penetrate me.
"Because even my own body has the form of the Śrīcakra," such is the prayer of the author of the hymn.

The meaning is: "May these [waters] enter just as cows—though in reality they are free from desire (*niṣkāmatva*)—enter quickly from the forest to the cow-pen, desiring, as it were, to be near their calves; 'like those longing' means like cows desiring the proximity of their calves. This is the very Vedic text.

The root of the procedures for the placement of the wheels (*cakranyāsa*) found in the tantras is that these very deities are to be placed within one's own body; thus it is said: "May all those Yoginīs make my body their abode."
The root of that [power] also arises from the correspondence between the mantra of the deposition of power (śaktinyāsa) and its indicative mark (liṅga).
Now, in order to teach the two lotuses distinguished by three circles that remain in the wheel of emanation (*sṛṣṭicakra*), he recites the fourth verse, beginning with "ūrdhvajvalat":
"Blazing upwards, its light is a flame; it is not darkness in front, nor is it horizontal; it is that ageless *rajas*. (4)
It has come to pass: these rays of light from the moon, which bring joy and delight, truly adorn the orb.

The fourteen-spoked [wheel] and the eight-petaled and sixteen-petaled lotuses exist one below the other. Likewise, above, there is only one outer circle surrounding the pericarp; thus, according to the doctrine of some, there are three circles. For this very reason, it is of the nature of the *jyeṣṭhā* [vowels].
Regarding the phrase "three circles" (*bhramitraya*) in the passage "four-cornered, the form of Vāmā,
three circles," the term *bhramitraya* functions as an indicator (*lakṣaka*) for two lotuses situated within the two intervening spaces of the three circles.

The explanation of the ancient teachers is appropriate. Even regarding the statement: "O Dear One, the two lotuses joined by three circles, consisting of Fire and Moon according to the Śāktas," this very same explanation applies. And those circles consist of the three qualities (guṇas) of Fire, Moon, and Sun.

By the description of the verse concerning the *prakṛti*, it should be understood that the two lotuses situated between them have also been described. As for the literal meaning, it will appear later in the context of the *sthiticakra* and the *uttaracakra*. First, *tamaḥ* (darkness) is indeed of the nature of the determined quality of *tamas*, and is named "Flame" (*jvalana*).
It became a circle of light;
by the qualification "blazing upwards," the nature of the flame as being like fire is confirmed.

Furthermore, by observing soot in the upper portion, its nature as darkness is confirmed; for this very reason, the indeclinable *vai* is used to dispel any suspicion of inconsistency in describing that which consists of light as being darkness. Beyond that is the horizontal circle of light, spreading out transversely.
Because it was red, it became the quality of *rajas*; and that took the form of the sun, since the upward and horizontal radiation of fire and the sun is perceptible. As the learned have said:
"The movement of the sun, whose charioteer is thighless, is horizontal; the upward flaming of the fire-eater is well known.
Thus, the qualifier "undecaying" (ajara) is intended to firmly establish its distinction from fire. Therefore—

*Modanaṃ* (delighting) means that which produces worldly pleasure. From the moon (*indu*), the circle of light (*jyotirmaṇḍala*) arose. By the word *ānanda* (bliss), its nature as consisting of the quality of *sattva* is expressed; for it is precisely that which abounds in *sattva* that manifests the bliss of Brahman (*brahmānanda*). *U. vai. iti* is used for gentle address. *Vai* [is a particle of emphasis].
Or, it has the sense of the particle *eva* (only/indeed). Thus, the three circles are drawn. These mothers adorn [it], making it beautiful.
The Śrīcakra is distinguished by pairs of lotuses situated within the intervals between the three circles.

The meaning is that [the deity] is not only capable of performing the task but is also not merely weary from meditation; the intention is that worship beginning with *mantra* and ending with *bindu* is intended for times of distress (*āpatkāla*).
To teach the ninth wheel, which consists of the subterranean chambers (bhūgṛha),
he speaks the fifth verse, beginning with "tisraścarekhā" (three lines).

(5) And there are three lines, the abodes of the earth, the triple heavens, possessing the three qualities and the three lights. This city is the fulfiller of all that fulfills; herein Madana [the God of Love] proclaims himself together with Madanī [his consort].

In other tantras, three circles are seen to be prescribed outside the two circles of the pericarp, beyond the two lotuses. According to that view, the phrase "and three lines" should be understood as referring only to these three circular lines; it does not [refer to anything else].
And this being so, it should not be argued that there is an inconsistency in describing three mandalas as remaining solely from the pericarp (karṇikā), because in the *Tantrarāja*,
outside the sixteen-syllable [mandala], there is a circular boundary-line (*maryādāvṛtta*) distinct from the eight-petaled circle.

For it is logical that this Śruti [text] is rooted in that [tradition] by virtue of its being an exposition thereof. The grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the phrase "the earth, the dwellings, the three lines" is an unstrained meaning. Those very [lines] are the "three heavens," consisting of the three worlds, because they are the abodes of the deities.

Or they are of the nature of heaven. They possess the three qualities (*triguṇa*), meaning they consist of the three *guṇas*; they are the triple luminosity (*triprakāśa*), meaning they consist of the luminosity of the three circles in the form of the sun, moon, and fire.

He concludes the description of the Śrīcakra with the word "etad" (this). Described in four and a half [verses], this city is like the City of Śrī—a wheel (*cakra*) that is the dwelling place of the Supreme Deity together with her retinue. It is for those who fulfill, that is, for those who completely satisfy the heart's desires of devotees.

It fulfills even Śiva, Viṣṇu, and the others; it fulfills all desires. Here, within this Śrīcakra, Madana is renowned as Śivakāmeśvara, and I am renowned as Śivakāmasundarī, through the expansion of various forms such as the *aṇimā* [powers] which are of the nature of my own rays.

The meaning is "she sports. Alternatively, there is a word division as *madanī ā*, where the suffix *ḍīṣ* is applied according to the rule for feminine forms derived from a masculine base (*puṃyogalakṣaṇa*).
