The grammatical connection is "they spread" (*āprathete*), because of the Vedic allowance that [a word] may follow even when separated by other words. All those divine forms which are found in various fields under different names in the Purāṇas and the Tantras belong to her.
In order to teach "it is so," he recites the sixth verse.
She is Madantikā, the proud one, auspicious, fortunate, and beautiful;
she is pure, modesty itself, contentment, and beloved; she is nourished, Lakṣmī, Umā, graceful, and ever-speaking.
Regarding the phrase "Madantikā": in the *Padmapurāṇa*, during the enumeration of the Devī-tīrthas, several forms are mentioned, such as Lalitādevī at Prayāga, and so forth;
[furthermore], she is named Maṅgalā in Laṅkā and Bhadrasundarī on Trikūṭa.
Mahālakṣmī is in the Karavīra, and Rumādevī is in Vināyaka.

"Nourishment in the Devadāru forest, intelligence in the Kaśmīra region, and likewise contentment in the land of the Lord of Vatsa"— these and other such forms [of the deity] are to be sought in their respective places.

The fourteen verses beginning with "madantike" are an illustration of Viśālākṣī and others in Vārāṇasī; the meaning is that whatever form of the Goddess it may be, she is indeed that very same one, even while she is prattling through it. This refers to the word "lālapanti."

"Another [author] says that the case-ending, being uttered after the nominal stem, serves as a qualifier for the meaning of the nominal stem; this is seen from its usage in the *Śābarabhāṣya*. Alternatively, [this refers to] fifteen syllables."
These are the fifteen deities. In this context, the Atharvaṇa recension reads "siddhimatī" instead of "śuddhimatī."
In order to prescribe the worship of the deity thus described,
he utters the seventh verse, beginning with "imā vijñāya" (having known these).

(7) Having realized this, they rejoice with the nectar of immortality, satiating their own seat with the flowing stream; they dwell upon the back of the great celestial vault and enter the supreme abode of Tripura.

Having understood this aforementioned supreme deity— having known it through its various specific distinctions and having undertaken its worship by means of approaching a guru, initiation, and so forth— having accepted it, [one should meditate].

Their own seat is the Śrīcakra, which is non-different from their own bodies; therein, they gladden— that is, worship with offerings such as satiation— the deity together with the surrounding retinue by means of substances transformed into nectar (sudhā) through the process of distillation, and thus they rejoice.
Having first abandoned the manifestation of objective objects,

they possess a non-conceptual mental modification (*nirvikalpa-vṛtti*) whose sole object is their own Self. They dwell upon the summit of the great heaven and enter the supreme abode of the three cities (*traipura*).
This is the meaning. The "rendering immortal" (*amṛtīkaraṇa*) is an elliptical expression for the other consecrations (*saṃskāra*);
that the presiding deity is Sudhādevī, as well as the consciousness (*saṃvit*), is understood from the wording of the consecration mantra.

"Completely purified by the refinement of mantra, it is called the nectar of the deity. Thus, in the Rudrayāmala, it is said that dwelling upon the back of the great celestial vault (the sky) is indicative of the fruits of the three kinds of human goals; it is the supreme abode of Tripurā.
But its true nature is that which is to be approached by the liberated;
by that, liberation is spoken of, meaning that they attain all desires and liberation—this is the sense. Thus, that omnipresent power is discerned as Brahman.
The wise have declared it to be of two kinds: with attributes (saguṇa) and without attributes (nirguṇa).
That which possesses attributes is to be practiced by those who possess passion, while that which is without attributes is for those who are free from passion.
She is the untroubled mistress of virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation; when worshipped according to the prescribed rites, she bestows all desired objects.
Thus it is stated in the *Devībhāgavata* as well. One initiated into the *Śrīvidyā* should,
by means of worshipping his own seat (*svapīṭha*) with material offerings, bring about all desires through the door of non-conceptual mental states (*nirvikalpa-vṛtti*).
The injunction results in the prescription of a subsequent meditation distinguished by [prior] meditation. In every respect,
this very Vedic text is the source for the specific injunctions found in the Kalpasūtras and other works, such as "the wise man should be initiated," and so forth.

Although "satisfying" (*tarpayantaḥ*) is heard as a qualification of the qualified agent (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*) following the word "having known" (*vijñāya*), it is connected as the instrument (*karaṇa*) for the realization of the fruit; thus, "those who give gold attain immortality."

Thus, because it does not have an unattained object and because there is no obstruction to the power of injunction (*vidhi-śakti*), there is no contradiction with its status as an injunction (*vidhitva*), even though it is a mantra. [For example: "One should sacrifice *kapiñjala* birds for the sake of spring; one should lead forward those who are seeking protection."

Because even mantras such as "āsyajānanto nāmacidviktana" and others are frequently accepted as being injunctive in nature, and because, in reality, the word *madanti*— just like the sentence concerning the *āgneya* offering— is to be interpreted as having the *leṭ* (subjunctive) mood, according to the principle of the section on the meaning of verbal roots (*bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*).

The instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) belongs precisely to the meaning of the verbal root *mā* (to measure), which denotes a specific mental modification (*vṛttiviśeṣa*) whose object is one's own self as non-different from the Goddess of Consciousness (*ciddevī*). That same [meaning] is also what is denoted by the term "inner sacrifice" (*antaryāga*), because the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) denotes a specific mental modification. As for the word *parisrutā*, however...
Through the indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*), it connects with the root-meaning;

or, by means of the principle of the "red one-year-old cow" (*aruṇaikahāyanīnyāya*), there is a subsequent connection (*pārṣṭhikānvaya*) between both [the root-meaning and the suffix-meaning] as they are already connected to the productive operation (*bhāvanā*). This is just like [the connection of the word] *pratiṣṭhanti* with *nākasya pṛṣṭhe*.

The passage beginning with "ityādi" serves to present the object to be realized (*bhāvya*), and because the word "ca" (and) expresses a conjunction of results, it possesses the character of a combined qualification (*saṃvalitādhikāra*), just as in the case of the statement: "He indeed becomes purified, radiant, an eater of food, possessed of sense-power, and rich in cattle. This applies to many [results].

The meaning is that the fruits [of the rites] function as a collective whole (*vyāsajyavṛtti*) for the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*). However, this is not like the case of "from all desires," where the satisfaction is individually sufficient; rather, according to the maxim of the fruitful and the fruitless, this [collective nature] is understood. But having understood this... [imāṃ vijñāyeti].

The property that delimits eligibility for learning (*vidvattā*) is [the specific qualification]. For this very reason, the traditional legal code (*samayācārasmṛti*) stating, "There is no eligibility for the twice-born who are devoid of family-initiation (*kuladīkṣā*)," is justified. Here, the phrase "while offering libations" (*tarpayantaḥ*)...

In the context of the external sacrificial rite (*bāhyayāgavidhi*) which is about to be described, [the word] "nivedayan" (offering) and "svātmīkṛtya" (having made one's own) are used with the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*) and the gerund suffix (*lyap*), respectively.
Since it is stated that the offering to the deities (*devatā-nivedana*) and the internal appropriation for oneself (*svātmīkaraṇa*) occur simultaneously,

the natural sense of the scripture (*śruti-svārasya*) applies only to the rite of divine drinking (*divya-pāna*), not to the rite of heroic drinking (*vīra-pāna*). Therefore, drinking is said to be of three kinds, according to the sequences of the divine (*divya*), the heroic (*vīra*), and the animal (*paśu*).
The divine drink was offered before the Goddess, and the Hero was honored at the conclusion of the rite.
Thus, another root Śruti for this Smṛti must be sought. As for the prohibitions concerning human ends (puruṣārtha),
since they apply exclusively to matters prompted by worldly desire (rāga-prāpta), they do not apply at all to those acts enjoined as being for the sake of the sacrifice (kratvartha).
By whatever means possible, one should fix the mind upon Śiva;
therefore, by whatever means possible, one should fix the mind upon Kṛṣṇa.
This is because such is the natural intention of these and other Puranic statements;

for therein, many clear declarations are found which, by virtue of their being for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*), enjoin [certain practices] with reference to all social classes (*sarvavarṇa*).

And since these [Smṛtis] are rooted in numerous direct Vedic revelations (*pratyakṣa-śruti*), there is no occasion for considering their relative strength or weakness; such is the direction of the argument.
Having thus enjoined the meditation on the external form, the author speaks the eighth verse with the desire to enjoin the meditation on the subtle form:
(8) "Desire is the womb."
Kamalā, Vajrapāṇi, Guhā, Hāsa, Mātariśvan, Abhra, Indra, and again Guhā, Sakalā, and Māyā— among these,
Puruṣī is the Mother of the Universe, the Primordial Knowledge (Ādividyā).
"Kāma is the source. Here, a fifteen-syllable mantra is extracted;

and because its deity is feminine and it is of the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*), it is designated by the term "Vidyā. Even though such a mantra is the Mother of the Vedas, the *Gāyatrī* is recited aloud [in the liturgy]. But of this [mantra]...
By the indication of only a few [syllables] without mentioning the words that express them syllable by syllable,
the extreme secrecy of the mantra is intimated, as well as the same quality of the rites pertaining to it through that [mantra]. What more need be said?

The *Tripurātāpinī* clearly demonstrates that even the *Gāyatrī* is indeed the extractor of the primordial knowledge (*ādividyā*); likewise, the first verse of the *Bhāgavata* also corroborates this very point: "We meditate upon that primordial knowledge which is the form of all consciousness."
"May He who impels the intellect from within."
This mantra is to be understood solely through the grace of the feet of the Lord of Gods (Devanātha), owing to its extreme secrecy.

It consists of: the syllable denoting Mātariśvan (the Wind-god) and Kāma; the syllable denoting Caturmukha (Brahmā); the fourth vowel and the eleventh vowel of Kamalāyoni (Viṣṇu); and Indra and Vajrapāṇi (Śiva).
The third is the semi-vowel (ya), the seed-syllable of Guhāmāyā Bhuvaneśvarī;
"abhra" is its first syllable, the letter *ha*; the remaining five [letters] constitute her essential form. This is the primordial Vidyā, ancient and vast, the Mother of the Universe.

The *Yoginīhṛdaya*, in its section on the meaning of the tradition (*sampradāyārtha-prakaraṇa*), describes in detail that the Mother of the World is the Vidyā because the world arises from her syllables; as for the meaning of the mantra, however, it has been explained in many ways by Dattātreya, Agastya, and others, according to various Tantric systems. That...

And this has been presented by us, having collected it from the *Varivasyā-rahasya* according to our own understanding; therefore, it should be understood from that very source. Having taught the Vidyā worshipped by Kāmarāja, he speaks the ninth Ṛc in order to teach the Vidyā worshipped by Lopāmudrā.
The sixth and seventh [are as follows].
(9) Teaching that the sixth, the seventh, and then the fire-charioteer (the Sun) are the three roots of this [system],
they declare [these] to be the one to be told (Kathya), the Seer (Kavi), the Fashioner (Kalpaka), Desire (Kāma), and the Lord (Īśa).
Those who offer praise partake in immortality.
The meaning is that one should uproot the primary triad— the first three syllables— of this very vidyā; and in their place,
one should insert the same three letters beginning with the sixth.

By means of either of the two vidyās of the Jāpaka, those who have praised— that is, are praising— the Lord, the Supreme Śiva whose limiting adjunct is pure sattva, and who are muttering [the mantra], attain immortality;
the meaning is that one should contemplate liberation through the muttering of the vidyā, [worshipping] the Lord.
He distinguishes [the Self] from desire— that desire which, as established in the section on "Icchati" (Icchādhikaraṇa), is presented by scripture as "May I be many, may I procreate"—
and from the "Kalpaka," the locus for the conceptualization of the universe, which was described in the section on "Janmādi" (Janmādyadhikaraṇa) as the "Seer" (Kavi).
The one who is to be described as the author of the Vedas and known through the Vedas— whose identity as the Supreme Brahman alone was stated in the two sections of the *Śāstrayonitvādhikaraṇa*—
is the meaning conveyed by the qualifying attributes; this is established by the marks of Brahman such as "undecaying" and "not ancient," and so forth.

In this context, a threefold meditation on the Supreme Deity is prescribed: by means of masculine forms and by means of feminine forms pertaining to the meditation on the Kāmakalā which is about to be described.
And thus it is further elaborated in the Kulārṇava:
"One should meditate on the Goddess in male form, or one should contemplate her in female form;
or else, one should meditate on her partless (niṣkala) nature, characterized by Being-Consciousness-Bliss."

Although it might be easily stated that there is a fixed rule— namely, that the formless (niṣkala) is the object of worship for others, the male form for recitation (japa), and the female form for external sacrifice (bahir-yāga)— nevertheless,
the equal primacy of both the female and the male will be explained hereafter.
And according to the tradition, this option alone is intended.
Although the extraction (*uddhāra*) of other vidyās worshipped by Manu, Candra, and others is also seen in the *Tripurātāpinī*, only the extraction of these two is presented here;
this is for the purpose of intimating their superiority. For this very reason, it is said in the *Jñānārṇava*:
Having extracted these twelve kinds of knowledge,
O auspicious lady, this pair of knowledges is difficult even for the gods to obtain.

This is further supported by such passages as these. Between these two [traditions], there is an implied suggestion of superiority for the Kādi-vidyā alone, because it is extracted first; for this very reason, it is said:
"Among mantras, the Śrīvidyā is indeed supreme, and therein the Kādi is like the Aparā."

Thus, we have established in our *Setubandha* commentary that this expansion of the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*— which speaks of a hierarchy among all the sciences (*vidyās*) despite their essential non-difference— is merely a form of praise. For this very reason:
The illustrious Ācārya Bhagavatpāda has demonstrated the reversal of these two in the *Saundaryalaharī*; even there, however,
for the sake of conforming to the present Śruti, the terms *Śiva*, *Śakti*, and *Kāma* have been interpreted otherwise.
The commentary on a few [passages] need not be respected because of their obscurity and lack of purpose; for here, since the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*) alone is the subject under discussion,
there is a conjunction of further qualities by way of restating its constituent substances.

Since the context continues because the *dvādaśī* [mantra] is to be prescribed, the recitation (*japa*) occurring within that [context] is a subordinate part of the internal sacrifice; therefore, they "attain immortality."

The statement "like the hearing of the *apāpaśloka*" is an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise). For even in the case of a mantra, there is no obstacle to accepting its status as an *arthavāda*, just as its status as an injunction (*vidhi*) is accepted.

However, in the case of [the mantra] "tisraḥ puraḥ" and so forth, although it is a supplement to the injunction for the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*), it does not have the nature of an *arthavāda*.
There is no evidence that being a supplement to an injunction (*vidhiśeṣatva*) is necessarily pervaded by being an explanatory passage (*arthavādatva*);

furthermore, even if it were an explanatory passage, it would possess authority regarding its own meaning as a statement of an existing fact (*bhūtārthavāda*). Moreover, the meditation on the "gross" (*sthūlopāsti*) in the twelfth verse is not at all distinct [from the subtle meditation].

It must be stated that [the meditation] is prescribed as having the form of an external sacrifice; nevertheless, because the conclusion is seen in the fifteenth ṛc through the explanation of the meaning of the verbal root *dhā* (to place), the continuity of the context is unavoidable. In reality, however, there are three meditations (*upāsti*).

There is indeed equal primacy; for since the result is heard in all three injunctions, there is no criterion for determining that any one of them alone constitutes the primary context (prakaraṇin). Furthermore, like the group of six sacrifices beginning with the Āgneya, they produce the result only when combined.
A householder should always perform both internal and external sacrifice:
the worship of the King of Wheels (Cakrarāja), the recitation of the Goddess’s mantra, and the chanting of Her names.
For a devotee, this much is the duty; they know anything else to be worldly prosperity.

This is because of such statements. Furthermore, the capacity of mere internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*) and recitation (*japa*) to produce results depends upon the specific qualified practitioner (*adhikāriviśeṣa*), as established by scriptural authority.
This is even so in the case of one who does not perform the Soma sacrifice, despite the absence of the *agnīṣomīya* sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).
The reasoning beginning with "as in the case of the accomplishment of the fruit" (phalasiddhivat) is to be inferred by those learned in logic. Thus ends the ninth verse.

Now, with the desire to prescribe the worship of the gross form, [the author describes] the specific gross form for the purpose of establishing within the wheel (cakra) that fundamental deity who has been meditated upon as possessing attributes internally.
He speaks the tenth ṛc in order to explain [it].
I praise that [reality] which is the triple heaven, the triple-faced, the center of the vowels within the nine lines of the Universal Mother.

The great lunar days (*bṛhattithi*), numbering fifteen beginning with the tenth, sustain that city of the Sixteenth (*ṣoḍaśī*) as the triple heaven (*triviṣṭapa*). Following the word *rekhā*, there is the elision (*praśleṣa*) of the vowel *visarga* of the sixteenth; [this occurs] within the nine lines—the nine *ghaṭikās* of the womb (*yonighaṭikā*)—[denoted by] *aḥ*.

Thus, that which has the middle [position] as its place of the vowel *a*; or alternatively, that which has nine lines—namely the *saṃhāracakra* (wheel of withdrawal)—and whose middle position is characterized by the vowel *a*;
or that in which the vowel itself is the syllable *aḥ*.
Alternatively, the analysis [of the compound] is *aḥ-ravara*; such is the "three-faced" triangle—
that is, the central triangle— which is the triple-heaven (*triviṣṭapa*), meaning the abode or the place of worship of Viśvamātā, Tripurasundarī.

Because heaven (*svarga*) is the abode of the deities, the place is indicated here by the word denoting it. "Tad īle"—this is the speaker’s statement; and having reached the middle of these two vowels, the *saṅkāra* becomes the letter *la*. Thus.
By the rule of the *Prātiśākhya*, the letter *ḍa* has become *la*.

This very *Upaniṣad* is also recited by the followers of the *Atharva-veda*; according to their view, there is no substitution of a "badly articulated" (*duḥspṛṣṭa*) sound—this is the established conclusion—precisely because it is stated that the vowel lacks a middle [articulatory] position.

By the principle that "the remaining fifteen vowels are equal to the point (bindu) because they are heard as equal across the three lines," their existence as being divided fivefold into five parts is implied. That triangle is large and clearly manifested.
The meaning is that [the deity] sustains the thirty-five lunar days— the deities of the fifteen lunar days—
namely the Nityās beginning with Kāmeśvarī and ending with Citrā; thus, five Nityās each are to be worshipped in their respective places along the southern, upper, and northern lines.
Having contemplated that [mandala] augmented in the Ocean of Knowledge,
one should subsequently draw five lines upon the great triangle in the sequence of the foremost, the right, and the left, according to the fivefold order.
One should contemplate the letters beginning with *a* and ending with *ḷ* on the southern [line];
then, on the eastern line, the five beginning with Dīrghakarṇa.
"Then, having drawn [the diagram], one should write the Śakti and so forth along the northern line;
in the middle, ending with the Anusvāra and including the Visarga, one should worship the Ṣoḍaśī. Thus it is said.
Indeed, those very fifteen digits characterized by the increase and decrease of the moon are the lunar days (tithis),
beginning with the new moon (darśa) and ending with the full moon (pūrṇimā); there are exactly fifteen such digits.

These are indicated in the Tantra by such passages as "seen, unseen, and the state of being unseen," and they are also recited by the Taittirīyas. The sixteenth digit (*kalā*), called *sādākhya*, which is devoid of increase and decrease, is the cause of these. And that—
Because she is the cause of the fifteen *nityās*, she is called *Ādinityā*.
That aforementioned Tripurasundarī, being the very nature of Ādinityā, dwells in— the middle of— the city, which is the Śrīcakra, specifically the locus of the sound of the *visarga*.

It should be understood that because the sixteenth vowel (*au*) manifests the *ha*-letter, which consists of the forms of *prakāśa* (light) and *vimarśa* (reflective awareness), it is logical for it to have that as its essence.
In this context, the eleventh verse is spoken in order to teach the meditation on the Kāmakalā, which is performed for specific desires (kāmya) and is based upon the external sacrifice (bahir-yāga).

(11) Having known the two circles, the two breasts, the single orb of the face, the three lower [regions], and the three abodes of the secret cave— the beloved digit whose form is desirable— a man becomes one who can assume any form at will and is himself desirable.
Regarding "two mandalas": two mandalas are the two breasts; one *bimba* is the face; three *sadanāni* are the houses on the ground; and the cave (*guhā*) is the form of the half-*hakāra*.
Although, according to the lexicon stating that "*bimba* is not feminine and *maṇḍala* is used in all three genders," the word *bimba* [is also applicable here].
This is the division of the three mandalas described in the fourth verse by way of being the "reciter of the mandala" (maṇḍalavācaka). Even there,
it is specifically the mandalas of Fire and Sun that constitute the two breasts, due to the inherent force of the word *bimba*.

From the order of recitation, it is clearly understood that the *bhūpura* situated immediately below that is indeed the half-*hakāra*. Furthermore, those various forms of the *kāmakalā* are clearly manifest, as they are pointed out in many places throughout the various Tantras. Nevertheless...
This is because of the corroborative statement by the venerable teacher (Bhagavatpāda):
"Having made the face the *bindu*, one should meditate on the pair of breasts below it, and below that,
the half of Hara."

Because the order of meaning overrides the order of the text, the word *bimba* refers to the *bindu*; being thus directed toward the *bindu*, it refers to the entire series of cakras beginning with the *bindu* and ending with the *mantra*.
The wheel, consisting of the three mandalas, has the nature of power and fire.

Thus, since in the *Sundarīśloka* the term "maṇḍala" is seen to be explained as referring to the wheels (*cakra*) such as the ten-spoked one, the word "one" (*eka*) is used for the purpose of contemplating the six maṇḍalas, beginning with the *bindu*, as a single integral whole.
The phrase "two maṇḍalas" refers to the two wheels of eight petals and sixteen petals; this should be understood thus.
This mention of three parts is an illustration intended to include all the constituent parts.
In reality, even in the body, there are only three parts: from the head down to the throat.

From the throat to the breasts, from the heart to the perineum (sīvinī), and from the hair to the hands and feet— these are its branches. Thus, she who has transformed into the nature of all the cakras, the beloved one (kāmī).

Having known—that is, having meditated upon and contemplated—the digit (kalā) belonging to Manmatha, whose essence is Kāmeśvara; that is, the digit of consciousness (citkalā), which has a desirable form, meaning a beautiful nature. "Having known" (viditvā) is the reading found in another recension [of the scripture]. The person (naraḥ) is the practitioner (upāsakaḥ); he becomes one who can assume any form at will (kāmarūpaḥ), like Manmatha.
One becomes instantly handsome and a disturber of all women.
He says "it is called *kāmya*" because this is stated too briefly; for since it is heard without qualification, its essential nature is one that is desired by all people within the three worlds.
As it was said by the venerable teacher (Bhagavatpāda):
He who meditates upon the art of love in the consort of Hara, [attains success].

"The moon, possessing a pair of breasts [the sun and moon], along with the ascetics and women who cause agitation to those who have attained [liberation], quickly causes even the three worlds to whirl about, for it is exceedingly light.
Thus it is said.
"One who desires the power to assume any form at will and the fulfillment of all desires should meditate upon Kāmakalā"—

this is an injunction establishing the relationship between a quality and its fruit. Here, since meditation— which is by nature an action— is enjoined for the sake of a result, it does not require another substratum [for its own existence].

However, because there is an absence of both the integration with the auxiliary parts of the Soma sacrifice— as in the case of the Śyenakratu— and the integration with the auxiliary parts of an external sacrifice,
the result arises from its performance even outside of an external sacrifice.
This is the intention of the venerable teacher (Bhagavatpāda):
"Having visualized the Bindu as the mouth, one should visualize the two breasts situated below it."
One should contemplate that lower half facing downwards.

If it is argued that the fact that this meditation has the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvarthatva*) is also recorded by the injunction situated in the section on sacrifices (*kratuprakaraṇa*) in the *Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava*, what follows from that? [The answer is:
nothing at all, just as in the case of the *Aveṣṭi* sacrifice, which has the desire for food and other such things as its fruit, those who seek such fruits perform it externally.
Because the application [of the practice] remains unimpaired, for this very reason it is stated in the Śāṇḍilya Bhakti-sūtra, beginning with the recollection of the Blessed One:
"The external and internal [forms of worship] are both [valid], like the Aveṣṭi and the Sava sacrifices."
In order to prescribe the substances for the external sacrifice and the procedure for those substances,
he recites the twelfth verse.
(12) By offering to the Great Deity liquor, fish, prime meat, cooked grains, and well-prepared roots,
the virtuous man, having made these his own, attains perfection.
Regarding the term *parisrutam*: *jhaṣa* means fish; *pala* means meat. *Parisrutam* is that which is first among the fish and meat; the meaning is that it is the second [item] following the first.
By this, fish is the third [item]: rice-grains (*bhaktāni*), as well as *vaṭaka*, chickpeas (*caṇaka*), and so forth.
Various kinds of food consisting of mung beans and so forth. The fourth term, "yonis," is an indicator for those born from a *kuṇḍa* or *golaka* womb; that is the fifth [category].
As for the plural form "yonīs," it refers to [women of] the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, and other castes.
This refers to the intention of a few specific types of *jāti*.

That [intention] is to be seen in the Tantras through the term "the group of eight *kalās*" (*kalāṣṭaka*) and so forth, which serves as its elaboration. The word "and" (*ca*) is intended to include all five [categories] collectively. Although *pala* is recited after *jhaṣa*, [it is nonetheless included].

Because they are placed at the beginning by the first word prior to *jhaṣa*, the intended sequence of the *makāras* is indicated. Therefore, according to the principle that when the primary [substance] is unavailable one may worship with substitutes, even if the five *makāras* are not obtained, there is still the performance of the daily ritual (*nityakrama*).

And although [the goal] is accomplished by means of the *Kalpasūtra*, it is indicated that if the preceding [means] are unavailable, one does not take up the succeeding primary [means], even when it is available.

Even when only the first measure is obtained, since the fourth is necessary for the purpose of the *naivedya* offering, taking that much alone is to be understood through the traditional practice (*sampradāya*). In the reading from another recension (*śākhā*) which says "clarified butter" (*ājyam*), the meaning is indeed ghee (*ghṛta*). In that context, it refers to that [ghee] by virtue of its being cooked.

The qualification applies to both [the *tantra* and the *vikāra*] according to the maxim of the crow’s eye (*kākākṣigolakanyāya*). However, the interpretation that it refers to "that which is connected to the *aja*" (the goat) is not tenable, because in the *Tantra* we observe the word used in the sense of "modification" (*vikāra*),
and because it would result in a restrictive enumeration (*parisaṃkhyā*) of only five [types of *tantras*], such as those mentioned in the Sūtra.

Even if one obtains only as much as is sufficient for the mere propitiation of the Supreme Deity (paradevatā), the sacrifice is not performed by means of a substitute; for in an external sacrifice, since self-identification is a form of consecration (pratipatti),
there is no impediment even if that [self-identification] is omitted, and so forth.
This should be inferred as established by the logic of the sixth [chapter]. They are well-refined, purified by both visible and invisible consecrations (*saṃskāra*);
and these consist of worldly types such as cooking and the like, as well as Vedic types such as the removal of curses and the like.
Many [of these] are well known in the tantras.

According to the maxim "whether much or little, as prescribed for one's own home," he may offer only the quantities mentioned in the *Kalpasūtra*; while performing the sacrifice (*yajan*), the virtuous performer of the external rite (*sukṛtibahiryāgakartā*) offers it to the Great Goddess, the Great Deity (*mahatyai devatāyai mahādevyai*), and having internalized those [offerings] within himself, he makes them his own.
Having himself also consumed [the offering], he attains— reaches— the *siddhi*, which is the fruit of the sacrifice; that is to say,

by means of a sacrifice characterized by the fivefold sequence beginning with the first [syllable] combined with one another, and dedicated to the deity Mahādevī, he should bring about the attainment of his desired goal (*iṣṭasiddhi*).
The manner of concluding the ritual procedure and so forth is to be understood as being exactly like the procedure for the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*).
The Lord spoke this verse from the *Trayī* (the three Vedas) in order to teach that meditation on the deity with attributes (*saguṇadhyāna*) is an auxiliary part (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice.
Like two hounds with a leash, the one who moves among all people binds those who approach him with a noose. With five arrows and a bow,
the innate power, ruddy and beloved by all, pierces them.

"With the goad, as if white"—here the instrumental case is used in the sense of a characteristic (itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇe). She is characterized by a goad (*sṛṇi*), which is like a hook (*aṅkuśa*); "white" (*sitayā*) means either made of silver or, because there is no distinction between "white" and "sharpened," it refers to one that is sharp-edged. Thus she is marked by such a goad.

Viśvajanyā—she whose progeny is the universe; the mother of the entire world, Aruṇā, possessing a crimson hue, the primordial power Mahātripurasundarī; Viśvacarṣaṇi—the beholder of the auspicious and inauspicious deeds of every living being; [she who bestows boons upon] those who are desirous.
He binds with a snare those who are lustful and, driven by craving and greed, proceed along this path;
having bound them with the snare, he pierces them with a bow and five arrows.

It means that it causes those devoid of craving to fall downward; however, as for the fact that it leads upward those who proceed with a discriminative intellect, this is already established by the injunction itself, and thus it is not stated again. As it has been said:
"One should practice [the path] with the understanding that it is a prescribed rule; if one does so out of craving, one is a sinner.
By the very same substances through which downfall occurs, liberation is likewise proclaimed.
Thus, these [rules] are established as applying both to one who desires [results] and to one who does not. And so forth.
Regarding the verse "Like a ploughshare" (*sṛṇyeva*), Yāska states that the ploughshare is of two kinds: the supporter and the destroyer.

The word "like" (*iva*), being connected everywhere [in the verse], indicates that while the qualified form (*saguṇarūpa*) is assumed for the sake of showing grace to devotees, it is the unqualified form (*nirguṇarūpa*) alone [that is primary].

It reveals the ultimate reality. Since that which possesses attributes is merely conceptualized, the fourteenth verse is spoken to teach the equal primacy of both female and male: "Bhaga is Śakti... and so forth.
Bhaga is power, Bhagavān is desire, and Īśa is the giver of both; here, among the Bhagas, they are equal in primacy, equal in essence, equal in fearlessness,
and equal in power— the undecaying source of the universe.
"Bhaga" is a synonym for "Vimarsa" (reflective awareness); it is defined as the sixfold totality consisting of sovereignty, dharma, fame, fortune, knowledge, and discernment.

By such Smṛti passages as these, the entire aggregate of attributes constituting the nature of Īśvara is indicated here by the word *bhaga*; that very collection of attributes is called *śakti*. [This refers to] her who is described in female form as the object of worship.

This is the true nature of the deity. As it is stated in the *Nāgānanda-sūtra*, having introduced the self-reflection (*vimarśa*) which constitutes the very nature of Brahman, whose essence is light: "This indeed..."
Discernment, consciousness, sentience, the Self, the supreme speech arising from its own essence,
the orientation toward the Supreme Self as absolute freedom, sovereignty, true reality, existence, radiance, the core, Mātṛkā, and Mālinī.
The wave of the heart is the vibration of one's own consciousness.
Thus it is proclaimed by such scriptural authorities as these.
A detailed exposition of these specific attributes of Dharma is to be found in their respective commentaries (*bhāṣyas*).

The Blessed One is indeed distinguished by such a collection of qualities. He is *kāma*, the Lord; he is *Kāmeśvara*. This alone is the masculine form of the deity to be worshipped. Here, through this worship, [one attains] fortunes consisting of the aims of life (*dharma*, *artha*, and *kāma*).
Both are bestowers of various fruits; the meaning is that through the twofold meditation on the qualities of a single deity, the three aims of human life (*trivarga*) are accomplished.

The term *sattva* refers to those whose primary quality (*pradhāna*) is equal; here the word *sattva* denotes a *guṇa*. Therefore, the meaning is that they have entered into a mutual relationship of *guṇa* and *guṇin* (quality and possessor of quality). Because Śiva serves as the substratum (*ādhāra*) in meditation by virtue of being the seat for Kāmeśvarī, he is the *guṇa*.
Śakti is the primary [element], because in the meditation on Śiva as conjoined with Ambikā as his half, she constitutes specific limbs such as the hands and head; thus, Śakti is the attribute (guṇa),
while the sense is that Śiva alone is the primary [substance].

Thus, although there is equality in the capacity to bestow the desired fruit and in the mutual relationship of subordinate and predominant qualities, the aspect of being the creator of the world resides solely within the Power (Śakti). Therefore,
indicating that the attainment of the fruit occurs swiftly through meditation on her very form as a woman, he says:

Regarding the phrase "of the two alone": it refers to the Goddess herself, who possesses equal power, who is the totality of all powers, and whose nature consists of the entire collection of attributes, situated between Śiva and Śakti in the form of Ardhanārīśvara, being perfectly merged with one another without distinction.
She is the source of the universe and the protectress of the world. Accordingly, the *Śaktisūtra* states:

"Consciousness is autonomous, the cause of the manifestation of the universe. Thus, the word *sama* (all) is well-known as a synonym for "everything," as seen in such passages as *uruṣyāṇo aghāyataḥ samasmāt* ("protect us from all who intend evil"). [The term] *ajarā* means...

The meaning is that, regarding the aspect of being the source of the universe (*viśvayonitva*), the qualification of being the creator of the world (*jagatkartṛtva*) is accepted because it is free from the stain of doubt, as it is established by means of valid cognition such as direct perception. This has been stated in the *Bhāgavata*:
Śakti creates the universe; she alone protects it entirely.
By her will, she destroys this world of the moving and the unmoving.
Neither Viṣṇu, nor Hara, nor Indra, nor Brahmā, nor even Agni [is its creator].
Neither Ārka nor Varuṇa are capable, in any way whatsoever, of performing their respective duties.
"For joined with her, those gods perform their respective duties;
she alone is the cause in their actions, as is perceived through direct observation. Thus [it is said].
Elsewhere it is also said:
"Even Śiva becomes a corpse when deprived of Kuṇḍalinī;
whoever is devoid of power is considered by the wise to be incapable."

Such details are to be seen in the *Setubandha*. Therefore, although Śiva possesses the capacity to bestow fruits and so forth, that capacity is delayed because it is dependent upon Śakti; however, for Śakti [it is otherwise].

The sense is that because [the female form] is independent [of external aids], it is "unhesitating"; therefore, for those desiring swift accomplishment, it is appropriate to meditate on the deity specifically in the form of a woman. Having thus explained meditation with attributes (*saguṇadhyāna*), since there is no portion of the subject matter remaining to be stated regarding meditation without attributes (*nirguṇadhyāna*), [the author speaks of] its resulting fruit.
And in order to teach the channel for its production, he recites the fifteenth verse,
beginning with "parisrutā."
(15) When the mind has dissolved from the contraction [of egoism] through the purified sacrificial offering of *parisrut*, it indeed flows forth.
Everyone is the creator, the sustainer, and the destroyer of the entire world; thus one attains the state of universal form.
Regarding the paths of action, the path of knowledge, and the path of devotion,
various distinct indirect means (*praṇāḍikā*) have been described by the founders of their respective scriptures; all of these [are as follows].
That "difficult to accomplish [rites] yield fruits over a long period of time" is indeed clear to those who know the various scriptures. In this context, however,
the channel [of attainment] is simply a succession of exhilarations produced by the repeated acceptance of substances.

In that regard, the duties prescribed by the rules of conduct (samayācāra) apply up to the limit of mature radiance (prauḍhollāsa); at the end of that radiance, there is freedom of action (yāthākāmya); and in the final radiance, there is the nature of Brahman itself.

And so says the Kalpasūtra: "In the stages of the commencement of youth, fresh youth, mature youth, its end, and the overflowing of the mind beyond that, the practice of the rule (samayācāra) extends up to the end of maturity; after that, one acts according to desire (yathākāmī)."

The characteristics of the seven joys (*ullāsa*) should be observed in the *Kulārṇava* and other such texts. Although the attainment of the nature of Brahman indeed occurs every day during the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*),
this is because at that time the mind has dissolved.

Nevertheless, because it is permeated by sleep—which is a specific transformation of ignorance—that state is not the goal of human endeavor (*puruṣārtha*). However, such a state when devoid of sleep is indeed the goal of human endeavor; it is that which is designated as the seventh stage among the stages of knowledge (*jñānabhūmikā*).

The wise consider that very state which yogis experience as non-conceptual samādhi (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*) to be the "unmanifest" (*unmanā*) and the "beyond" (*uttara*), even in the *Ullāsa* [of the *Trika* scriptures], where it is said: [The text continues: "That which is experienced by yogis as non-conceptual samādhi is indeed the state of *unmanā-uttarā*. Thus it has been stated.
"Bliss is the form of Brahman, and that is established within the body;
the substance that manifests it is drunk by the yogis. Thus [it is said].
In the Kalpasūtra, however,
it is stated that the five *m*s (pañcamakāra) are its manifestors.

However, if that very same substance, which is a constituent part of a material sacrifice, is drunk while being impure, then— being obstructed by the sin resulting from the inclination toward an act prohibited for the person— it is not capable of producing that [spiritual] state, provided it has been purified by mantras.
Indeed, it is the very form of the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) that produces the state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*). As it is said in the *Samayācārasmṛti*:
"The unrefined drink of the bound soul (*paśu*) causes quarrel, agitation, and evil."
Indeed, that which is devoid of mantra and worship is merely the drinking of a beast.
Even a hero, having drunk according to the rite of animal-sacrifice liquor (paśupāna), may go to hell;
however, that which produces awakening when consecrated acts as both an expiation and a means of purification.
Through that radiance of the mantras, great sins are destroyed;
by drinking the consecrated [substance], one gains longevity, prosperity, beauty, good fortune, and knowledge.
The eightfold sovereignty and the power of moving through the sky occur when one falls [from the body] according to the prescribed rite.
In the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice and in the Kula tradition, a Brāhmaṇa may drink wine;
elsewhere, having drunk it, a Brāhmaṇa must perform an expiation.

And so forth. However, it is better that one's life-breaths depart than that a Brāhmaṇa should offer liquor; for by drinking intoxicating liquor, a Brāhmaṇa falls away from his very status as a Brāhmaṇa.
Because this has been prohibited by such statements as those in the *Śaktisaṃgamatantrarāja* and other scriptures,
the means for casting off the fetters of dharma (dharmapāśa) must be understood here solely from the oral tradition (*sampradāya*).
The various modes of systematic arrangement have been demonstrated by us in the *Kaulopaniṣadbhāṣya*. Consequently, for those qualified for that [system],
through such exultations, [the state] of that which is delimited by the internal organ—
When the contraction of the individual self (*jīvātman*) caused by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is removed,
what remains upon attaining the state of Brahman?
Nor can one achieve the goal of life merely through that [state], since the manifestation of a substance is subject to coming and going.

This must be addressed, for this objection applies equally even to the case of meditative absorption (*samādhi*). Now, in that case, through means such as the regulation of breath (*pavana-niyamana*) and by entering into absorption again and again, one attains proficiency through long-term practice; thus, after a few days have passed, [the result occurs] even without [external effort].
If it is argued that "the cessation of the breath gives rise to a concentration (*samādhi*) that persists at all times,

because we observe that for those traveling by boat upon the ocean who have been rocked for a long time by its waves, the rocking continues even after they have disembarked from the boat," then the same [principle] applies here.
The same applies to the subject at hand as well.

Even without the substance, through proficiency in the practice of the state of *unmanī* born from the drinking of refined substances, such an unartificial condition is accomplished within a few days. As for the literal meaning, it is [attained] by means of purification (*pāvitena*).

When the contraction of the self— the sense of limitation arising from the internal organ (*manas*)— has dissolved and vanished without re-emergence, through the oblation consecrated by mantra-rituals which remains as the residue of the Goddess’s worship, and through the *parisrut* being drunk; and when [that contraction] has melted away.
This means: in the state that transcends the expansion of *unmanī*. "Vai" signifies with certainty that everyone becomes the self of all.
Therefore, intoxication (*mada*) is that which generates a non-conceptual mental state (*nirvikalpaka-vṛtti*) whose sole object is one's own nature.
Thus, in the sentence prescribing the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*), it is concluded that this refers to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*).
With this very intention, the manifold nature of what is considered "intoxication" (*matta*) in the *Tantra* is established.
Lustful men, being intoxicated, take their pleasure; the wrathful, being intoxicated, become angry;
singers, being intoxicated, sing; and yogis, being intoxicated, engage in meditation. Thus it is said.
By this, the specific yoga is also implied as being an auxiliary to this [state]. He explains his very nature as the self of all:
he alone is Brahmā, the creator of the entire world; he is Viṣṇu, the sustainer;
and he is Rudra, the destroyer. What need is there for more?

He says that he becomes one whose form is merely all living beings, such as slaves, fishermen, and others, by stating "he attains the state of universal form" (*viśvarūpatvam eti*). However, as for the falling away of the body, let it happen whenever and wherever it may due to the force of *prārabdha*; it does not matter for him.
What is the distinction? The sense is that [he] has accomplished all that was to be done (*kṛtakṛtyatva*). And it is said in the *Kalpasūtra*:

"Having understood this and having performed the rites according to the rules, for one who is devoted to his lineage, there is a state of having accomplished everything in every respect; upon the casting off of the body, there is no difference between a dog-eater’s house and Kāśī."
"He is one who is liberated while living."
Thus, while concluding the statement of the Tripurā-siddhānta, [the author] recites this sixteenth verse ending in *yajus* in order to teach that there is also fruit from its study: "This..."
"The Great Upaniṣad."

(16) This is the Great Upaniṣad of Tripurā, whose imperishable syllable is praised with supreme words. She is the Ṛg, she is the Yajus, she is the supreme Sāman, she is this Atharva, and she is every other branch of knowledge. Thus ends the Upaniṣad.

And this has been further augmented by the venerable Śrī Paraśurāma, the author of the Kalpasūtras, who said: "Whoever studies this Mahopaniṣad consisting of ten sections, which constitutes the entire essence of the Great Tri-pura Siddhānta, [he shall be successful] in all..."
"He becomes a performer of sacrifices in all sacrifices; whatever ritual he studies, by that very one his sacrifice is performed"—so indeed it is heard in the Upaniṣad. May there be auspiciousness!

By this [statement], those required meanings that have not been explicitly stated in this *Mahopaniṣad* are to be taken from the *Kalpasūtras*; for it was with reference only to those capable of synthesizing the scattered chants belonging to various Vedic branches that the section on the *Kalpasūtras* [was established].
Thus it is established by virtue of the support for the authority of the *prayoga-śāstra*.
As for the literal meaning: this *Mahopaniṣad* of Tripurā, which consists of a collection of sentences revealing the secret [teachings], is to be recited—this is the ellipsis.
He states the reasons for this with the words beginning "yām" (which...), [referring to] the Supreme Imperishable, Brahman, as the agent.
This *upaniṣad* which one praises with words—that is, with words of praise; [the form] *riṭṭe* is from the root *ṛḍ*, meaning "to praise. In the word *parame*, *so* is substituted for *saḥ*.
[The phrase] "which is Brahman" is formed by the transposition of the two words.

Or, by accepting the fact that it ends in the first and second [case endings], it is a praise (*stu-ti*) of Brahman as its object, composed by the author of the Upaniṣad; the meaning is that this is because it has been praised even by the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), and because it is laudatory of Him. [She who is] Tripurā, whose syllable is *hṛllekhā*...
Or, it means "he praises. Alternatively, there is a word division as *paraṃ e* (the supreme *e*), meaning the syllable in the form of the vowel *e*. Or:
"That seed-syllable which is the eleventh support, arising from the three corners, by which the universe—from the Egg of Brahmā down to the outer shell—is seen even today. Thus [it is said].
Because of the scriptural statement.
Even in the case of the vowel *e*, there may be a division as *a* and *i*.
For it is heard in scripture: "In space, indeed, is all speech; he hears it, O Alaka," thus it is said, "he hears."

Alternatively, the final *oṃkāra* is construed as qualifying the [inexpressible] syllable (*akṣara*). The meaning is that it—the supreme, indivisible [Reality]—is praised by the "speech-syllables," namely *a*, *u*, and *m*.
"Whether taken as a whole or individually, one who seeks refuge utters the word 'Om'";
thus it is remembered in the *Śivarahasya*. Furthermore, there are also various forms of study prescribed by the injunction "One's own Veda (svādhyāya) is to be studied."

He says "this" (*eṣā*) to show that [the goals] are accomplished by the study of this very [text]. The words *ṛk* and so forth refer to the Vedas as a whole, and not to individual mantras, because they occur in a context where the *Atharva* and others are the primary subjects.
The words "this," "that," and "this one" (*eṣā*, *etat*, *ayam*) refer to the *Ṛg*, *Yajus*, and *Atharvaṇa* [Vedas].

This is with the intention of [the Sāman] being the qualificand. Since the Sāman consists of sound and thus lacks syllables (*anakṣara*), the word "as if" (*iva*) indicates that it yields a result equal to that of the syllables.
By taking four from among the eighteen branches of knowledge (vidyās), the other fourteen, such as the Upavedas and so forth, are included by the word "others."
The meaning is that this Upaniṣad is the very nature of all things.
He states "Om" to show that this [Upaniṣad] is also the very nature of the Praṇava. By the rule *omāṅośca*, there is a single substituted form (pararūpa);
the intention is that it should therefore be recited even by ascetics (*yatins*).

With the intention that "this Upaniṣad is of such a nature," and that even the Śruti itself is unable to directly express the greatness of one who knows its greatness— because he is of the very same form as Brahman and because speech does not function therein— the Śruti [says]:
"Maintaining silence—this is the Upaniṣad. The sense is that there is no further secret portion remaining to be spoken. Thus [ends] the Śrī.
Thus, by Bhāskararāya, who has kindled the fire of knowledge, some of the meanings of the Tripurā Mahopaniṣad—
which though unfit to be revealed, have been told for the satisfaction of the learned.
Thus ends the commentary on the Tripuropaniṣad composed by the venerable Mahāśaya Bhāskararāya.
"May my speech be in my mind"—this is the peace invocation.
The Śrī Lalitā Mahātripurasundarī Upaniṣad.

The Goddess, who is the knower of the *Bahvṛca-veda*, sat with one-pointed concentration. She alone created the cosmic egg; she is known as Kāmakalā and is known as Śṛṅgārakalā. From her alone Brahmā was born.
Viṣṇu brought it forth; Rudra brought it forth; all the hosts of Maruts brought it forth;
the Gandharvas, Apsarases, and Kinnaras, playing musical instruments, brought it forth from every side;
they brought forth that which is to be enjoyed; they brought forth everything; they brought forth everything consisting of power (śakti).

Whatever is born from an egg, born from sweat, born from a sprout, or born from a womb—whatever living being exists here, whether stationary or moving, including human beings—this is that Supreme Power (Parāśakti). This is that Śāmbhavī Vidyā; it is the Vidyā beginning with *ka*, or the one beginning with *ha*.

Whether called *vidyā* or the *sādi*, whether called *vidyā* or the *rahasya*, Oṃ Oṃ is established in speech. That very [consciousness], pervading the three cities and the three bodies, illuminating both the external and the internal,
is indeed the Great Tripurasundarī— the inward-facing consciousness— due to its non-attachment to space, time, and objects.

That alone is the Self; everything other than that is unreal and non-Self. Therefore, this realization of Brahman is free from the categories of existence and the agent of existence; it is the primordial consciousness, the non-dual realization of Brahman, a wave of Being-Consciousness-Bliss.
Mahātripurasundarī, having entered within and without, shines forth as the one alone.

That which exists is pure Being (sanmātra); that which shines is pure Consciousness (cinmātra); that which is dear is Bliss (ānanda). All this is Mahātripurasundarī in every form—both you and I, and everything.
The universe consists of all the deities; everything else is Mahātripurasundarī. Truth is the single reality known as Lalitā; she is the non-dual, indivisible Supreme Brahman.
Through the relinquishing of the five forms and the abandonment of non-essential nature,
the supreme substratum— the one great Reality— remains as that which is truly existent.
It is expressed as "Consciousness is Brahman," or "I am Brahman.
It is indeed spoken of as "That thou art. Or it is said, "This Self is Brahman," or "I am indeed Brahman," or "Whoever I am, that I am," or "I am He."
That which is expressed as "I am He" (yo'sau so'hamasmi) is this very sixteenfold Śrīvidyā,
the fifteen-syllabled Mahātripurasundarī; she is known as Bālāmbikā, or Bagalā, or Mātaṅgī, or Svayaṃvarakalyāṇī, or Bhuvaneśvarī.
She is Cāmuṇḍā, Caṇḍā, Vārāhī, Tiraskariṇī, Rājamātaṅgī,
Śukaśyāmā, Laghuśyāmā, Aśvārūḍhā, Pratyaṅgirā, Dhūmāvatī, Gāyatrī, Sāvitrī, and Sarasvatī.
The bliss of Brahman.

In the imperishable syllable of the Ṛgveda, in the highest heaven, upon which all the gods are seated—whosoever does not know that, what will he do with the Ṛgveda? But those who know it, they sit here together.
Thus ends the Upaniṣad. "May my speech be in my mind"—thus [is] the peace invocation.
Thus ends the Lalitā-Mahātripurasundarī Upaniṣad belonging to the Bahvṛca Veda.
"Even those who recite the Atharvaveda attain the supreme goal," thus it is stated in the Nāgara-khaṇḍa.
The Atharvaśīrṣa Upaniṣad of the Goddess.
Oṃ, "May we hear with our ears what is auspicious," thus [is] peace.

Oṃ. All the gods indeed approached the Goddess and said: "Who are you, O Great Goddess? She replied: "I am the embodiment of Brahman. From me proceeds the universe consisting of Prakṛti and Puruṣa; I am both the void and the non-void; I am bliss and non-bliss."
"I am consciousness and unconsciousness; I am Brahman and non-Brahman"—thus says the Atharvaṇa Śruti. "I am the five elements and that which is not the five elements;
I am the entire universe. I am the Veda and that which is not the Veda; I am knowledge and ignorance."
I am the born and I am the unborn; I am below, above, and across.
I move with the Rudras, the Vasus, and with the Ādityas and all the Viśvedevas. I support both Mitra and Varuṇa; I [support] Indra and Agni, and I [support] both the Aśvins.
I bestow Soma, Tvaṣṭṛ, Pūṣan, and Bhaga;
I bestow Viṣṇu of the wide stride, as well as Brahmā and Prajāpati.
I bestow wealth upon the one who offers oblations, the skillful sacrificer who presses the juice.

I am the sovereign ruler who gathers together all treasures; upon the summit of this world, I bring forth the Father. My source is within the waters, in the ocean. He who knows this attains the station of the Goddess. Those gods said: "Homage to the Goddess, the Great Goddess!"

Constant salutation to Śivā! Salutation to Prakṛti, to Bhadrā; may we, being self-restrained, be ever bowed down before her. To that goddess Durgā, who is fire-colored, blazing with ascetic fervor, the daughter of Virocana, and who is honored for the fruits of actions—to her [be salutation].

I take refuge in her who utterly destroys darkness—the Goddess Speech whom the gods brought forth; she whom creatures of every form speak. May that Cow, Speech, yielding for us gentle food and vigor, protect us with her well-sounding praise.
We bow to Kālarātri, praised by Brahmā, the power of Viṣṇu, the mother of Skanda, Sarasvatī, Aditi, the daughter of Dakṣa—the purifying and auspicious one.
We know Mahālakṣmī; may we meditate upon all-perfecting success. May that Goddess [grant it] to us.

May she impel us. Aditi was indeed born, she who is your daughter, O Dakṣa. After her were born the gods, the auspicious ones whose kin are the immortals. Kāma, the womb, Kamalā, the wielder of the thunderbolt, Guhā, Ha, Sā, Mātariśvan, Abhra, Indra, and again Guhā.
Furthermore, she who is the Mother of the Universe, possessing all [powers] through her illusory power (māyā), is the primordial wisdom;
she is this very self-power (ātma-śakti), the deluder of the universe, bearing the noose, goad, bow, and arrows—she is the illustrious Mahāvidyā. Whoever [knows her thus...]
One who knows this crosses over sorrow. Homage be to you, O Blessed One;
O Mother, protect us from all sides. She is these eight Vasus;
she is these eleven Rudras; she is these twelve Ādityas; she is this...

The Viśvedevas are both drinkers of Soma and non-drinkers of Soma. This [universe] consists of Yātudhānas, Asuras, Rakṣasas, Piśācas, Yakṣas, and Siddhas. This consists of the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas.
This consists of Prajāpati, Indra, and Manu. This is that.
I perpetually bow to her who takes the form of time— consisting of the planets, constellations, luminaries, kalās, kāṣṭhās, and so forth; to the Goddess who removes all suffering,
who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, who is infinite, victorious, and pure.

The seed-syllable of the Goddess, which provides refuge, bestows auspiciousness, and is auspicious herself; joined with the letter *vi* (the sky) and the letter *ī*, endowed with *vītihotra* (the letter *ra*), and adorned with a crescent moon—this single-syllable mantra accomplishes all aims; thus [it is taught] by the ascetics.

Those of pure mind, consisting of supreme bliss and being oceans of knowledge, meditate upon Him; therefore, He is endowed with six faces, including the one whose nature is speech, illusion, and Brahman.
The Sun (Ra) joined with the left ear (Va) and the bindu (Ṃ), followed by the third letter from Ṭa (Ḍha); joined with Nārāyaṇa (Na) and Vāyu (Ya) conjoined with the lower lip (U);
and Vi (Vi)—this nine-syllabled mantra shall bestow great bliss.
I worship her who dwells in the center of the heart-lotus, radiant as the morning sun, the daughter of Sūrya,
holding a noose and a goad, with hands granting boons and fearlessness,
three-eyed, clad in red garments, and the fulfiller of the desires of her devotees; I bow to her.
I [worship] you, the Goddess, the destroyer of great fear.
She who pacifies great calamities and embodies supreme compassion; since even Brahmā and the other gods do not know her true nature, she is called "The Unknown" (Ajñeyā).
Since no end to her is found, she is called "The Infinite" (Anantā). Regarding her apprehension...

Because she is not perceived, she is called "unperceivable" (alakṣyā). Because her birth is not perceived, she is called "unborn" (ajā). Because she alone exists everywhere, she is called "one" (ekā).
Because she alone possesses manifold forms, she is called "not one" (naikā). Therefore...
Thus she is called the unknowable, the infinite, the unperceivable, the unborn, the one, and the many.
She is Mātṛkādevī of the mantras, the embodiment of knowledge of all words; she is beyond the consciousness of all cognitions, the witness of the void among all voids—she whose...
There is nothing higher than her; she is proclaimed as Durgā. Because she protects one from difficulties (durga), the Goddess is called Durgā. I seek refuge in the Goddess;
O Dudurgā, remove my sin! [I bow] to that Goddess Durgā, who is difficult to attain.

I, fearing worldly existence, bow to her who destroys misconduct and carries one across the ocean of saṃsāra. Whoever studies this Atharvaśīrṣa obtains the fruit of reciting all five Atharvaśīrṣas. This is the Atharvaśīrṣa.

He who performs worship without knowing [this] does not attain success in the worship, even after reciting it a hundred lakhs of times. The prescribed rule for the *puraścaraṇa* (preliminary rite) of this [mantra] is one hundred and eight recitations.
He who recites it ten times is immediately liberated from all sins.
By the grace of Mahādevī, one crosses over great difficulties.
Studying [this] in the evening destroys the sin committed during the day;
studying it in the morning destroys the sin committed during the night.
By practicing [this recitation] every morning and evening, one becomes free from sin;
by reciting it at midnight, during the fourth twilight (turīyasandhyā), perfection of speech is attained.
By reciting it before a newly consecrated image, the presence of the deity is established.
By reciting this during the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (the ritual installation of vital breath), the establishment of the vital breaths occurs.

He who knows this and recites it on an *Aśvinī* day under the influence of Mars in the presence of Mahādevī crosses over great death. This is the Upaniṣad. Om, "With auspicious ears..."—thus the peace mantra (*śānti*).
Oṃ tat sat.
Thus ends the Devyatharvaśīrṣa Upaniṣad.

The Śrīkaulopaniṣad and its commentary: Oṃ! May the Kaulika be auspicious to us; may Vāruṇī be auspicious to us; may purity be auspicious to us; may Agni be auspicious to us; may everything be auspicious to us; all has become auspicious.
Bhāskararāya, whose heart-coverings have been dispelled by the spreading rays from the lotus-feet of his venerable Guru,
causes the Kaulopaniṣad of the Atharvaveda to blossom.

In order to dispel the inevitable obstacles that arise when teaching the extremely secret meaning about to be explained, he prays to the deities with the verse beginning "May there be auspiciousness for us,
O Kaulika," and so forth.
May the Kaulika, the Supreme Śiva who initiates the path of the Kula,
who bestows the bliss of one's own Self after first dispelling obstacles— He who is the first presiding deity of Vāruṇī— be present for us.
May the Great Deity also be auspicious to us; may the Deity presiding over purity, the second [tattva], also be auspicious to us;
may Agni, the fire, be auspicious; and what need is there to say more—may everything be a source of happiness.

Salutation to Brahman; salutation to the Earth; salutation to the waters; salutation to Agni; salutation to Vāyu; salutation to the gurus. You alone are the manifest [Brahman]; you indeed are she. I shall speak of you alone as the manifest; I shall speak of her as the *ṛta*; I shall speak the truth.
I shall speak; may that protect me, may it protect the speaker; may it protect me, may it protect the speaker. Om. Peace, peace, peace.
Salutations to the Supreme Brahman, to the deities of the fourfold elements beginning with earth, and to the lineage of gurus starting from Paramaśiva down to one's own teacher.
The four elements, including space, are also implied. That Brahman which is directly perceived through the guise of the notion of "I" and is experienced by all—that indeed is You;
that very same [Brahman] is You. This is because of the *Kaulopaniṣad* in the form of Tripurasundarī. Therefore, O...

I shall declare that you alone are the Kaulopaniṣad, being non-different from it. The word *ṛta* refers to Brahman; the word *satya* is likewise. The repetition [of *ṛta*] is out of reverence; the rest is clear. "Peace! Peace! Peace!"—this is a prayer for the pacification of obstacles.

Now, therefore, the inquiry into Dharma. Knowledge and wisdom are "jñāna," and knowledge is the sole cause of liberation (*mokṣa*). Liberation is the realization of the identity with the Self of all. The five sense-objects are the phenomenal expansion (*prapañca*); their true nature is that of the Knower. Yoga is liberation.

Now, since the knowledge of the substratum has arisen immediately after the desire to know Brahman, inquiry must be undertaken for the sake of knowing the nature of Dharma through the power of reflection (this is the meaning).
Knowledge (*jñāna*) and intellect (*buddhi*): direct, immediate experience of Brahman is *jñāna*;
that which produces it, namely verbal [knowledge], is indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*), which is *buddhi*.
As in such passages as: "He whose intellect proceeds toward reality until it culminates in direct experience. Etc.

The meaning is that, because both types of conventional usage are observed, both of these are indeed the very nature (svarūpa) of dharma. By the use of the word "ca" (and), there is the inclusion of unmentioned attributes such as consciousness (caitanya) and others enumerated by [the author of] the *Nāgānanda* and so forth.
Acceptance. Knowledge is the sole cause of liberation; the meaning is clear.

Liberation is the accomplishment of the state of being the Self of all. The state of being the Self of all is the non-difference of everything from one's own Self; its accomplishment is the cessation of ignorance, along with its manifestations, regarding that [Self]. Therefore, the entire [meaning] of the half-verse of the *Devībhāgavata* has been stated.
It is implied that the knowledge having the same meaning as "This alone is indeed the eternal; there is nothing else" is the producer of liberation.
Or rather, [liberation arises from] the undivided mental modification (*vṛtti*) produced by such knowledge.

He explains the term "all" by stating that "the five sense-objects are the manifold (prapañca). The pentad of sense-objects, beginning with sound, is denoted by the word "manifold," because the gross elements are non-different from those subtle elements.
"Because even the thirty-six principles (tattvas) are included therein, the five elements exist everywhere, and there is nothing else as a sixth"— thus it is stated in the *Vāsiṣṭha*.

Having thus indicated the insentient class with the words "whose nature is knowledge" (*jñānasvarūpāḥ*), he now indicates the sentient class: "He is both knower (*jña*) and life (*ana*)," meaning that he knows objects through knowledge and breathes [sustains life]. In other words, the individual souls (*jīvas*) have such a nature. Yoga is liberation (*mokṣa*).
Yoga is the cessation of mental fluctuations; liberation, too, is this.
The very ignorance regarding the cause of unrighteousness is itself knowledge.

Because it is devoid of attributes (*dharma*), *adharma* is the Supreme Brahman; that which is the ignorance regarding its cause is precisely the fundamental ignorance (*mūlājñāna*) concerning that [Brahman], and that very thing is knowledge—the word "only" (*eva*) is placed out of its logical order (*bhinnakrama*). The objects are the individual souls (*jīva*), and [their] union...

The meaning is that all this—liberation, ignorance, and so forth—is nothing other than knowledge; there is no such thing as [anything] distinct from Śakti. The intention is that difference is false. This applies even to the relationship between the governed and the governor, which pervades the difference within the Lord (Īśvara) and the phenomenal world (prapañca).
Because it is false by virtue of the perception of what is incompatible with the pervader,
the Lord is indeed the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). Even impermanent things such as pots, which appear as permanent due to their impermanence, [are likewise unreal].
It is indeed of the nature of eternal power;
ignorance is knowledge,
and even ignorance, being of the nature of a state, is indeed of the nature of knowledge.
The meaning is that it is simply power (śakti).
Non-dharma itself is dharma.

Even dharma, which is of the nature of power (*śakti*), is not a separate category of reality (*padārthāntara*); rather, it is Brahman itself, whose nature is the substratum of attributes (*dharmin*) possessing those attributes.
This is liberation (*mokṣa*).
This alone is the path to liberation; there is no other.
The five bonds are of the nature of consciousness.
The notion of self in what is not-self, the notion of non-self in what is the self, and so forth—such cognitions alone constitute bondage. This is because of the *Śivasūtra*: "Cognition is bondage.
Furthermore, there is the mutual differentiation among individual souls (*jīva*), the differentiation from the Lord (*Īśvara*), and the differentiation from pure consciousness (*caitanya*).
Thus, there are five together with the three types of knowledge.
Birth from a physical body.
It is precisely because of the existence of such bondage that birth, in the form of connection with the microcosmic egg (piṇḍāṇḍa), occurs.
Liberation is found in that very state.
However, by the power of the knowledge of the Kaulas, even liberation occurs right there, within that very physical body (*piṇḍāṇḍa*);

there is no longer any delay in the form of departing through more than a hundred channels, traveling by the path of the gods (*devayāna*), or attaining liberation together with Brahmā. For him, it is exactly thus...
"His vital breaths do not depart for a long time," and so forth, according to another Vedic scripture.
This is knowledge.
Having first stated the established doctrine of the scripture, he declares the essence of knowledge:
"this" refers to the treasury of all knowledge that is about to be described.
Of all the sense organs, the eye is the foremost.

One should lead back to Brahman. Even in the individual cognitions produced by all six sense organs—cognitions such as "I know this"—wherein that which appears as the "I" (ahantā) is the primary reality, it is Brahman alone. That very [Brahman]...

For the Śruti states, "Everything shines only after it has shone," thereby declaring that everything other than That [Brahman] merely reflects its light. One should strive so that such discernment occurs in all mental modifications (vṛttis), even those produced by a single sense organ.
One should lead the primary element (pradhāna) by means of knowledge through the mantra of discernment.

The meaning is that, as stated in the verse: "While the cognition of the grasped and the grasper is common to all embodied beings, this distinction [in humans] consists in attentiveness toward the relationship [between them]," the very absence of non-discrimination is the entire essence of knowledge.
Actions contrary to the Dharma should not be performed.
From this point forward, he instructs on the manner in which a lay practitioner (*upāsaka*) should act.

For the sake of stabilizing the mind and so forth of those who take singular delight in being the locus of such discerning knowledge, one should practice the service of *saṃvit* and the rest even at the time of ritual action.
It is not proper to act in contradiction to the Dharmaśāstras.
Those who have not performed the duties prescribed by the Dharma.
Even those [rites] such as the Jyotiṣṭoma prescribed by the Dharmaśāstras are appropriate to perform when there is the possibility of such an obstruction to the flow [of life].
This is an authorization regarding both performance and non-performance, and not an absolute injunction or prohibition; for even by Gautama,
the forty sacraments (saṃskāras) were enumerated.

Having described the eight external and internal [disciplines], it was stated that after internal purification, the external ones are no longer necessary. Likewise, Manu, after describing all duties in detail, enjoins the practice of Brahman at the conclusion of the treatise.
For those intent upon that [liberation], disregard for the previously mentioned duties has been stated. This very Śruti is the source of such Smṛti.
Everything has the form of Śambhavī.

For there is no difference in the contemplation (*bhāvana*) of Tripurasundarī whether one performs what is prescribed or what is prohibited. The sense is that bondage arises from the performance of injunctions and prohibitions only for those who have fallen away due to a lack of such contemplation. Therefore:
The words of the Blessed One.
"If there should be a lapse in the ritual duties of men performing my work, thirty million great sages shall perform those rites for them. Thus [it is said].
The traditional scriptures do not exist.

Because it is already known, even the Vedas do not operate with respect to it. For this very reason, the venerable teacher [Śaṅkara] stated in the *Adhyāsa-bhāṣya*: "The scriptures have as their object those who possess ignorance. This was said in the two sūtras consisting of a concession (*abhyanujñā*) and a statement of purpose (*hetvarthavāda*).
The Guru is one.

This goal is attained through the worship of a single Guru characterized by the aforementioned qualifications; for if there were a multiplicity of Gurus, there would be a discrepancy in the instructions.
Because doubt is inevitable; for this very reason, it is stated in the Paraśurāmakalpasūtra:
"Worship of a single guru is free from doubt."
"Having properly obtained a family preceptor, one should not resort to another preceptor. Thus it is said.

This scripture is the source for the prohibition stated in the Kulārṇava. By the very statement "having found," the passage from the Śaktirahasya, "there are infinite gurus in the Kaulika tradition," intends to refer to the case where such a guru is not available.
Those who possess the cognition of the oneness of all things.

The word *aikyam* is formed by adding the suffix *ṣyañ* in its own sense (*svārthe*). Proceeding in this manner, even a practitioner (*sādhaka*) attains only the realization of non-duality (*advaitabuddhi*) at the time of death.
Because of the accomplishment through mantras.

This is the introduction. The meaning is that from this point forward, those rules (dharmas) which are to be practiced prior to the attainment of mantra-siddhi are being described. Therefore, the implication is that if even one of the rules to be mentioned hereafter is disregarded, there will certainly be a loss of siddhi.
Intoxication and the like should be abandoned.
Intoxication (mada) is a specific disorder produced by the consumption of the ingredients of a sweetmeat (modaka).
The group of six internal enemies (ariṣaḍvarga), which are to be grasped by terms such as "the end of transformations" (vikārānta) and so forth, must indeed be abandoned.
However, after the attainment of mantra-siddhi, desire, anger, and the rest do not manifest of their own accord.
As for specific transformations, they were already permitted previously. And thus:
As long as the gaze does not waver, one should drink the substance down to the throat;
since there is no contradiction between these two statements, as they are established as referring respectively to the practitioner of mantras and the one who has mastered the mantra.
One should not make oneself manifest.

Those who lack initiation into and devotion to their own mantra, who show extreme disregard for other dharmas, and who are mere semblances of practitioners of their own mantra— all such outward-looking individuals should conceal their practice in such a way that they would not be recognized as "a practitioner of this [mantra]."

And this is the same even in other initiations (*dīkṣā*), because of such statements found in their respective contexts as: "Those who are uninitiated do not look upon him while he is observing his vow," and so forth.

Although its secrecy is established simply because this initiation is prescribed in the *Āraṇyaka* section of the Vedas— just like the *Pravargya* rite which is an auxiliary part of the sacrifice (*kratvaṅga*)— nevertheless, its prescription is stated once again explicitly so that it may be distinguished from other secret rites.

This is for the sake of distinguishing [this case] from other dharmas: while in other dharmas the breaking of a secret results merely in a deficiency of the sacrifice (*kratuviguṇya*), here, if that occurs, it leads directly to hell. Thus said the venerable Paraśurāma: "From making [the secret] manifest, there is hell."
One should not engage in conversation with a paśu.

"All those who are outward-turned are indeed *paśus* (bound souls) because they are devoid of *vidyā* (knowledge); for this very reason, the term 'learned' (*vidvat*) is not applied to one who possesses knowledge of crafts and the like. From such statements [it follows that] together with them... [properly...]
One should not speak until one's own heart has been made known;
by this, there is no prohibition against speaking at first sight.
Injustice is justice.
Even if some sophist should disparage the Kaula practice by means of the principles of the Pūrva- and Uttara-mīmāṃsā, one should not feel even the slightest anger;
with this intention, he says: "anyāya" (unjust), where the negative particle *nañ* has the sense of "little," meaning a weak argument.
